docs.title: DevOps Infrastructure as Code with IBM Bob
i. "Infrastructure as code" paradigm for modern platforms
docs.text:
Christopher Bienko (AI Enablement GTM Product Manager) introduces the DevOps Infrastructure as Code with IBM Bob curriculum for hands-on enablement. [4 min]

Most production platforms today are built and operated through automation. Instead of configuring servers by hand, teams describe the desired state of their infrastructure in code and let tools make reality match that description. This practice is known as Infrastructure as Code (IaC).

Two of the most widely used tools are Terraform, which provisions infrastructure, and Ansible, which configures it. This lab uses both, together with Rancher Desktop, which provides the container engine.

RANCHER vs. DOCKER — WHY THE MIXED NAMING CONVENTIONS?

You install one piece of software on the server: Rancher Desktop, running headless (no graphical interface, because the server has no desktop). It ships a daemon binary called rdd, which is what the Ansible role installs and what systemd runs.

Rancher Desktop provides a Docker-compatible container engine. That is why, throughout this lab, you still type docker ps, Terraform still uses the kreuzwerker/docker provider, and the socket is still /var/run/docker.sock. "Docker" here names the interface, not a second product. Nothing in this lab installs Docker Desktop or Docker CE.

So when you read these pages:

When you see It means Rancher Desktop the software installed on the server — installing it, its systemd service, its VM, its version rdd the literal daemon binary and systemd unit name, nothing more Docker the interface Rancher Desktop exposes — the docker command, Docker networks and volumes, restart policies, /var/run/docker.sock, the kreuzwerker/docker provider

If a sentence is about what is installed, it says Rancher Desktop. If it is about what you type or what the code declares, it says Docker. There is no third thing.

Even with mature tooling, building a platform still involves real challenges:

  • Designing an architecture that is secure by default
  • Keeping code modular, idempotent, and reviewable
  • Handling secrets without leaking them into code or state
  • Reasoning about drift, blast radius, and rollback
  • Producing runbooks and documentation that stay current

It is precisely these challenges that IBM Bob was designed to address.

This lab is designed for DevOps engineers, platform engineers, SRE teams, and cloud architects. Anyone comfortable with a terminal can follow along, however.

docs.title: ii. What is IBM Bob?
docs.text:
IBM Bob is an AI-powered software engineering partner that supports the entire development lifecycle. Where a traditional code-completion tool is anchored to the moment of writing code, Bob is designed to support the lifecycle around it. Bob helps teams:

  • Design architectures from requirements
  • Generate infrastructure and application code
  • Review its own work for security issues
  • Deploy and validate systems
  • Produce diagrams, runbooks, and CI/CD wiring
  • Troubleshoot and operate what it built

RECOMMENDED PREREQUISITE: CLIMBING THE AI MATURITY CURVE WITH IBM BOB LEVEL 3

This course is best taken after the Climbing the AI Maturity Curve with IBM Bob Level 3 curriculum. It assumes those concepts are familiar ground: the Agentic Sidebar and its modes, the plan-first delegation discipline, and the review-before-trust habit that carried through every stage of that course. The material ahead builds directly upon that foundation.

Bob operates directly within the development environment, so you keep complete visibility into every stage of the process.

Throughout this hands-on lab, you give Bob a one-paragraph requirement and end with a working web platform running on a remote Ubuntu server. Bob designs the architecture and writes the Terraform and Ansible. It then reviews that code, deploys it, and proves that it works. Your job is to steer it with prompts and to judge the results.

docs.title: iii. Environment: the web platform
docs.text:
The platform you build in this hands-on lab is four containers on a private Rancher Desktop network, provisioned by Terraform and configured by Ansible.

Component Responsibility Traefik v2.11 Reverse proxy. The single entry point that receives every incoming request and routes it to the right backend service. It also publishes metrics about the traffic it handles. Docs Apache 2.4 The application. The classic open-source web server, here serving a landing page behind Traefik. Docs Prometheus Metrics store. A time-series database that collects metrics by scraping HTTP endpoints. Here it scrapes Traefik, so you can see request rates and response codes over time. Docs Grafana Dashboards. Turns metrics into charts. It arrives pre-provisioned with Prometheus as a datasource and a ready-made dashboard for the stack. Docs

This is the standard production pattern. A proxy sits in front and the application behind it. Metrics are collected from the traffic, and dashboards are layered on top.

The defining constraint: nothing is publicly exposed. Every container binds to 127.0.0.1 on the remote host. The cloud security group allows only SSH inbound. You reach the services from your laptop through SSH tunnels (ssh -L), and secrets live in Ansible Vault rather than in code or Terraform state.

Best practices built into the code, each verified during the lab:

  • Idempotent Ansible playbooks. Running them a second time changes nothing, which you confirm with make idempotency
  • Modular Terraform (network, traefik, web, monitoring), so each piece can be changed independently
  • A health check and restart policy on every container. In Module 3 you kill a container and watch Rancher's restart policy bring it back
  • Full rebuild from code alone. No configuration lives outside the repository

docs.title: iv. Architecture
docs.text:
The lab uses two machines: your laptop and one remote Ubuntu server. Everything runs on the server, inside four containers. Your laptop only sends commands and displays the dashboards.

Note, however, that the server has no web ports open. Its firewall blocks every incoming connection except SSH on port 2223. To reach the dashboards, you run an SSH command that forwards a few local ports (like localhost:8080) to the server, so the web pages travel inside the SSH connection instead of over the open internet. The diagram below shows that path.

FOLLOW ONE REQUEST

You open http://localhost:8080 in your browser. The SSH client picks the request up and carries it, encrypted, through the tunnel to the server. There it hands the request to 127.0.0.1:80, where Traefik is listening. Traefik routes it to the Apache container, and the page comes back the same way. To your browser it all looks local. The only thing that ever crossed the internet was SSH traffic.

HOW TO READ THE DIAGRAM

There are three parts, read from top of the diagram to the bottom:

  1. "Your Laptop" (left box): where you sit. You browse to normal-looking addresses like http://localhost:8080. Those pages are not served by your laptop: an SSH command you'll run during the lab forwards those ports over to the server behind the scenes.

  2. "Cloud Firewall" (middle): the server's only door. It lets SSH in (port 2223) and blocks everything else, so none of the web services are directly reachable from the internet.

  3. "Remote Ubuntu Server" (right box): where everything actually runs. It has two layers:

    • The 127.0.0.1 row lists the ports the containers are published on. 127.0.0.1 means "this machine only": those ports answer the server itself (and your SSH tunnel, which arrives as the server), but never the outside world.
    • The private Rancher network at the bottom holds the four containers. The arrows show who talks to whom: Traefik passes web requests to Apache, Prometheus pulls metrics from Traefik, and Grafana reads its charts from Prometheus.

docs.title: vi. What you will build
docs.text:
A WORD ON WORKING WITH GENERATIVE AI

IBM Bob is powered by generative AI and LLMs, and a defining trait of these systems is that they are non-deterministic — unlike the deterministic tools most developers are accustomed to. In practice, that means the same prompt can produce different code from one run to the next. This is both a strength and a quirk of the technology, and it is something to work with rather than against.

Precision is what tips the odds in your favor. The more clearly you describe what you want, the more closely Bob's output will mirror your intent; conversely, the smallest change in wording can meaningfully change the generated code. Throughout this lab, your results may differ from the solutions shown — and that is expected, not a defect. Whenever an output diverges, you have three good options: refine the prompt and try again, edit the generated code by hand, or simply proceed if the variation still compiles and runs. Human review remains essential at every step, and never more so than while you are still learning the tool.

You always stay in control. Bob proposes the architecture, generates the code, and runs the deployment. At every step, however, you review and approve what it produced before anything touches the server. This is the same discipline you practiced throughout the AI Maturity Curve course.

The lab repository begins with little more than a README file and the two workshop walkthroughs. Everything else is written by Bob during the lab, then reviewed and approved by you.

The code (Module 1). Using Bob IDE, you will build:

  • An architecture document with a diagram
  • Modular Terraform: network, traefik, web, and monitoring modules
  • Ansible roles that install the container engine and render every service config
  • Secrets encrypted with Ansible Vault
  • A security and compliance review of the generated code
  • Log aggregation with Loki and Promtail added to the monitoring stack
  • A disaster recovery runbook
  • A GitHub Actions pipeline, plus a Makefile that runs the same checks locally

The platform (Module 2). Using Bob Shell, you deploy that code to the remote server. Bob bootstraps the host with Rancher Desktop and creates the network and containers with Terraform. It then renders the configs with Ansible, opens the SSH tunnels, and validates every endpoint. The result is the four-container stack from section iii, live and reachable from your browser.

The proof (Module 3). You then operate what you built. You read the Grafana dashboards and query Prometheus. You kill a container and watch it self-heal, and you run a recovery drill from the runbook Bob wrote.

docs.title: i. WHAT YOU WILL DESIGN
docs.text:
Christopher Bienko (AI Enablement GTM Product Manager) provides an overview of the Design - Architecture and Planning module for the hands-on enablement. [2 min]

AI MATURITY CURVE

This module is the plan-first delegation discipline of Module 2 | Delegate, applied to infrastructure. Bob proposes in Plan mode, you review, and only then does Agent mode write files. Every sub-task carries its own approval gate, and every check Bob runs on its own work needs your consent before it executes. The scope is larger than anything in the previous course; the rhythm is the same one you practiced there.

In this module you hand Bob IDE a one-paragraph requirement and guide it through four steps:

  • Step A: turn the requirement into an explicit architecture
  • Step B: generate the Terraform layer (network, containers, volumes)
  • Step C: generate the Ansible layer (host bootstrap + content)
  • Step D: audit the result for security and secrets issues

Everything happens in Bob IDE on your laptop; nothing touches the server yet. Deployment is Module 2. Your job at every step is the same: paste the prompt, read what Bob produces, and approve it only when you are satisfied it matches the requirement.

docs.title: The requirement
docs.text:
This single paragraph is the entire specification the platform gets built from:

We have a fresh Ubuntu 22.04 server reachable only via SSH. No other inbound ports are open and the cloud security group cannot be changed. We need a production-grade containerized web platform: Traefik as reverse proxy, Apache serving a custom landing page, Prometheus for metrics, and Grafana for dashboards. Every container must bind to 127.0.0.1 (never 0.0.0.0) so access is exclusively through SSH tunnels from the operator's laptop.

docs.title: ii. STEP A: UNDERSTAND THE GOAL AND SKETCH THE ARCHITECTURE
docs.text:
Before writing a single line of code, you need an overarching picture of what you are building. That is what this step produces: a component diagram, the request and metrics flows, and the list of variables and secrets.

  1. Open the lab assets folder within the Bob IDE.

  1. Copy and paste the following prompt below into Bob's Agentic Sidebar chat, then hit Enter to execute:

    We have a fresh Ubuntu 22.04 server reachable only via SSH at $TARGET_HOST:$SSH_PORT. No other inbound ports are open and the cloud security group cannot be changed. I want a production-grade containerized web platform deployed by code: Traefik 2 as the reverse proxy with access logs, an Apache 2.4 container serving a custom landing page, Prometheus for metrics, Grafana for dashboards (admin password from a variable). Every container must bind to 127.0.0.1 on the host (never 0.0.0.0) so the only way to reach them is through ssh -L tunnels from the operator's laptop. Everything runs on a private Docker network with named volumes and a healthcheck on every container. Describe the target architecture, the request flow from the operator browser through the SSH tunnel into the host loopback into Traefik into Apache, the data flow for metrics, and produce a Mermaid component diagram that explicitly shows the SSH tunnel boundary. Then list the variables, secrets and outputs we will need.

These decisions are already made. Implement them and do not ask me about them:
- Host bindings, all on 127.0.0.1: Traefik web entrypoint 80, Traefik dashboard 8080, Grafana 3000, Prometheus 9090. The operator forwards high local ports (8080 to 80, 8081 to 8080); never a local port below 1024, which needs root on the laptop.
- Traefik routing: one router with rule PathPrefix(`/`) on the web entrypoint, service http://apache_web:80. No Host() rule — the operator arrives through the tunnel as localhost, which no Host rule matches.
- Images, pinned explicitly, never :latest: traefik:v2.11 (stay on 2.x for the file provider, not Traefik 3), httpd:2.4-alpine (Alpine is required — the self-healing demo needs busybox pidof), prom/prometheus:v2.53.0, grafana/grafana:11.1.0.
- Prometheus is reachable on 127.0.0.1:9090 for direct PromQL, not internal-only.
- No Apache metrics. Do not add apache_exporter or Blackbox Exporter. Traefik and Prometheus are the only scrape targets; Apache is measured by Traefik's per-service counters.
- The Grafana dashboard is a minimal custom JSON written for this stack, never a community dashboard ID.

docs.title: Enhancing the prompt
docs.text:
1. Click the sparkle icon to enhance the prompt.

  1. Bob breaks the one-paragraph prompt into a structured spec. The critical constraint is called out on its own, followed by a numbered list of deliverables: the diagram, the request path, the metrics topology, the variables and secrets, the SSH posture, and the limitations.

    Your enhanced prompt should look something like:

    Analyze the requirement above and produce a complete platform design for a single-host, multi-container web stack on Ubuntu 22.04 that includes Traefik 2 as an L7 reverse proxy with structured access logs, restart-on-failure policy and file provider configuration, an Apache 2.4 backend serving a Jinja-templated landing page, a Prometheus instance scraping Traefik metrics, a Grafana instance with a pre-provisioned datasource and starter dashboard whose admin password is sourced from a Terraform variable, and a Docker user-defined bridge network isolating all containers with named volumes for Grafana, Prometheus and Traefik certs.

Critical constraint: every published port MUST bind to the host loopback (ip = "127.0.0.1" in the Docker provider ports block) — nothing on 0.0.0.0. Operator access is exclusively via ssh -L localPort:127.0.0.1:remotePort tunnels from the laptop.

Produce:
(1) a Mermaid C4-style component diagram with a clearly labelled SSH-tunnel trust boundary between laptop and host
(2) the end-to-end request path browser -> ssh tunnel -> host loopback -> Traefik -> Apache
(3) the metrics scrape topology (all in-host loopback or container-network, never internet)
(4) a complete table of Terraform variables (target_host, ssh_user, ssh_port, ssh_private_key_path, grafana_admin_password, traefik_local_port, grafana_local_port, prometheus_local_port, traefik_dashboard_local_port)
(5) Ansible group_vars and required secrets with owner and rotation policy
(6) the minimum SSH posture on the host (key-only, no password auth)
(7) the explicit non-goals and known limitations of a single-host, tunnel-only design (no public TLS, single SPOF, operator must be online to demo)

docs.text:
1. Switch Bob's mode to Plan.

  1. Hit Enter to instruct Bob to execute the prompt.

docs.title: Bob's response
docs.text:
1. Approve the create-plan skill once. This is Bob asking permission to run its planning skill, which writes the design as a plan document you can review, instead of a plain chat reply. Approving it builds nothing yet.

  1. Bob scans the lab folder, finds only the three workshop files (a clean slate), works out that the entire platform must be designed from scratch, and starts writing the plan.

  1. Bob writes the platform design document, recording each key design decision with the reason behind it.

  1. The plan markdown file is now visible in the lab directory.

    YOUR RUN MIGHT NOT MATCH THE SCREENSHOTS WORD-FOR-WORD

    Bob phrases things differently on each run; what matters is that every item in the checklist below is present.

    IF BOB OFFERS TO IMPLEMENT THE WHOLE PLAN

    After writing the plan, Bob may ask you to pick an option to start implementing everything in one shot. Once the plan is done, click the stop button to end the prompt's execution. Implementation starts in Step B.

    IF BOB STILL STOPS TO ASK A DESIGN QUESTION

    The prompt above pins every decision Bob normally asks about, so it should go straight to the plan. If a run asks anyway, the answers are in that list — and the general rule behind them is use the fewest containers, export only what your two scrape targets actually provide, and pull nothing from an external catalog.

    Two answers cost the most if given wrong. Never add an Apache exporter: Traefik's per-service counters already measure Apache, and scraping mod_status gives Prometheus HTML it cannot parse. And never accept a community Grafana dashboard: they ship in HTTP-API format wrapped in {"dashboard": {...}}, which file provisioning rejects with "Dashboard title cannot be empty", leaving you with no dashboards at all.

    Because you are in Plan Mode, Bob responds with a design document rather than code. It contains a written architecture description and a Mermaid component diagram. It also lays out the request and metrics flows, along with a table of the variables and secrets the build will need.

docs.title: What to check before moving on
docs.text:
Bob's design should contain all of the following:

  • A Mermaid component diagram with the SSH tunnel drawn as an explicit trust boundary
  • The request path: browser → ssh -L tunnel → host loopback → Traefik → Apache
  • A metrics topology that never leaves the host: Prometheus scrapes Traefik over the container network, and Traefik and Prometheus itself are the only two scrape targets — no Apache exporter
  • A table of variables and secrets: host, user, port, key path, Grafana admin password, local tunnel ports
  • Honest limitations: no public TLS, a single host is a single point of failure, and the operator must be online to reach the stack
  • The container engine is named as Rancher Desktop, not Docker CE, and the design still uses Docker networks, Docker volumes and the kreuzwerker/docker provider

docs.title: iii. STEP B: GENERATE THE TERRAFORM LAYER
docs.text:
This step generates the Terraform half of the platform: what exists on the server, the private Rancher network, the four containers, their volumes and port bindings. What runs inside all of that (web pages, dashboards, configs) is Ansible's half, generated in Step C.

  1. Copy and paste the contents of the following code block into the Agentic Sidebar. Since it is long, Bob may show it as a collapsed window — click the "copy" icon next to the text block to ensure you've captured the entire statement.

    Generate a Terraform layout under infra/terraform/ using the kreuzwerker/docker provider configured against the remote container engine over SSH (ssh://${SSH_USER}@${TARGET_HOST}:${SSH_PORT}, identity file from var.ssh_private_key_path, with ssh_opts -i <key> -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no -o UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null -o IdentitiesOnly=yes). The engine is headless Rancher Desktop (the rdd daemon), which runs Moby's dockerd underneath and speaks the same Docker API, so this provider needs no Rancher-specific configuration — the Ansible bootstrap role exposes its socket at the standard path for exactly that reason.

Create modules: network, traefik, web, monitoring. Each module owns its own resources and outputs.

Critical implementation rules:
(a) the root versions.tf AND every modules/*/versions.tf must declare kreuzwerker/docker in required_providers - without this, Terraform silently looks for the non-existent hashicorp/docker and init fails
(b) every container ports block MUST set ip = "127.0.0.1" so nothing is exposed to the public interface
(c) every container resource must include lifecycle { ignore_changes = [log_opts, user, working_dir, command] } because the Docker daemon's daemon.json log-opts and the image's USER/WORKDIR defaults appear as drift on every plan and trigger needless replacements
(d) for Traefik specifically, do NOT use the docker provider auto-discovery - modern Docker Engine (25+) requires API >=1.40 but the Traefik docker client library starts at 1.24 and the daemon refuses the handshake. Instead use the file provider (--providers.file.directory=/etc/traefik-dynamic --providers.file.watch=true) with the routing config rendered by Ansible, mounted read-only. Mount it at /etc/traefik-dynamic, not inside /etc/traefik, because a bind mount nested under another mount in the same directory fails unpredictably. This is also better for the security review (no Docker socket exposure)
(e) for the web module's container, set init = true so Docker injects tini as PID 1 - needed so the self-healing demo in Part 2 actually works (Linux protects PID 1 of a PID namespace from SIGKILL, so without init=true httpd-as-PID-1 cannot be crashed from inside the container)
(f) every bind-mount source is an absolute path on the remote host, and always a directory, never a single file. The daemon resolves mount sources on the server, so path.module and path.root point at nothing; and Docker creates a missing file source as a directory of that name, which kills the container with "not a directory: Are you trying to mount a directory onto a file"
(g) every container sets restart = "always", or the self-healing demo in Part 2 has nothing to demonstrate
(g2) every healthcheck must call a binary that exists in that image. httpd:2.4-alpine ships no wget, curl, nc or busybox, so the usual wget-based test fails forever on a container that is serving correctly and Docker marks it unhealthy. Check what the image contains before writing the test; if it has no HTTP client, use a check that depends only on what is there
(h) Traefik's entrypoints inside the container are web on :80 and traefik on :8080. Two entrypoints on the same port make Traefik exit at startup with "error opening listener: address already in use". Add --ping=true so its own healthcheck answers
(i) Traefik access logs must go to stdout: --accesslog=true with no --accesslog.filepath. Promtail tails container stdout, so a filepath sends the access log to a file inside the container where Loki never sees it. Leave the format at its Common Log Format default

Ansible renders the host files that Terraform mounts, so both layers must name the same paths. Mount these directories, read-only:
/opt/lab/traefik/dynamic       -> /etc/traefik-dynamic
/opt/lab/web                   -> /usr/local/apache2/htdocs
/opt/lab/prometheus            -> /etc/prometheus
/opt/lab/grafana/provisioning  -> /etc/grafana/provisioning
/opt/lab/grafana/dashboards    -> /etc/grafana/dashboards

Name the containers traefik, apache_web, prometheus and grafana, because Part 2 addresses them by name. Publish on the host loopback at Traefik web 127.0.0.1:80, Traefik dashboard 127.0.0.1:8080, Grafana 127.0.0.1:3000, Prometheus 127.0.0.1:9090; those are the ports Part 2 tunnels to, and they are not the same numbers as the laptop-side ports. apache_web publishes nothing and is reached only through Traefik on the private network. Declare grafana_admin_user defaulting to "labadmin" alongside grafana_admin_password.

Use terraform.tfvars.example for inputs (target_host, ssh_user, ssh_port, ssh_private_key_path, grafana_admin_user, grafana_admin_password, domain) and never hardcode secrets. Generate outputs.tf exposing the localhost URLs operators will hit through the SSH tunnel (e.g. http://localhost:8080 for the app, http://localhost:8081 for the Traefik dashboard, http://localhost:3000 for Grafana, http://localhost:9090 for Prometheus) plus a tunnel_command output that prints the exact one-line ssh -fN -L ... command. The code must pass terraform fmt -check and terraform validate. Include a short README with init/plan/apply commands.

  1. Switch Bob's mode to Agent so it can write files.

  1. Hit Enter to execute the instructions.

docs.title: Infrastructure generation
docs.text:
1. Bob generates a todo list and asks you to approve it. This is Bob's work plan for the whole step, and it is worth reading item by item because it shows how Bob translated the prompt into work:

    SUB-TASK OBJECTIVES Sub-Task 1 Generate the Terraform layout under infra/terraform/ Sub-Task 2 Create the root module: versions.tf, variables.tf, main.tf, outputs.tf, terraform.tfvars.example Sub-Task 3 Create the network module: the private bridge network lab_net that every container joins Sub-Task 4 Create the traefik module: the reverse proxy container and its certificate volume Sub-Task 5 Create the web module: the Apache container with init = true from rule e Sub-Task 6 Create the monitoring module: Prometheus and Grafana, each with a data volume Sub-Task 7 Validate that every module declares kreuzwerker/docker in required_providers (rule a) Sub-Task 8 Validate that every ports block has ip = "127.0.0.1" (rule b) Sub-Task 9 Validate that every container has a lifecycle ignore_changes block (rule c) Sub-Task 10 Run terraform fmt and terraform validate

    Note the shape: create first, then validate against the prompt's own rules. Approve the list and Bob works through the items in order, ticking each one off.

  1. Bob starts with the root module. It asks to create the infra/terraform/ directory and the root files. These are the provider constraint (versions.tf), every input (variables.tf), and the wiring that calls the four modules (main.tf), together with the outputs and terraform.tfvars.example. The approval card shows each file's contents. Skim them, then approve to let Bob write them to the workspace.

  1. Bob scaffolds the modules/ directory next, the four folders that will each own one piece of the platform, starting with their versions.tf files (rule a from the prompt: the kreuzwerker provider must be declared in every module, or terraform init fails in Module 2). Approve to create them.

  1. Bob writes the network module. It holds a single resource, the private bridge network lab_net that every container joins, plus an output the other modules use to attach to it. Approve to create it.

  1. Bob fills in the three remaining modules (traefik, web, monitoring) and the README. This is the bulk of the code: the container resources with their 127.0.0.1 port bindings, healthchecks, volumes, and lifecycle blocks. Approve to create them.

docs.title: Validation checks
docs.text:
With the files written, Bob verifies its own output. Every check is a shell command, and each command needs your approval before it runs. The exact sequence varies by run; in this run Bob discovers Terraform is not installed locally and falls back to lighter checks.

  1. The first check is terraform fmt -recursive -check, a read-only formatting pass. Because it is a shell command, the IDE asks for an extra approval: check I understand the risk, then approve. Every check from here on needs the same confirmation.

  1. Then the cross-reference checks: three of them run in sequence, each proving one half of the module contract holds.

    • Every var. reference inside a module is declared in that module's variables.tf.
    • Every module.X.Y reference in the root matches an output module X actually declares.
    • Every argument the root passes into a module block is a variable that module accepts.
    • Bob wrote these checks itself. Read the commands before approving — this is Bob defining what "validated" means, then proving it.

  1. A final listing confirms the layout is complete, Bob closes out its todo list, and the infra folder appears in the lab directory: everything you just approved is now on disk.

docs.title: Review the generated files
docs.text:
1. Expand the infra/terraform/ folder to see everything Bob created.

    One module per component:

    infra/terraform/
├── versions.tf                  <- root provider constraint
├── variables.tf                 <- all inputs incl. port vars
├── main.tf                      <- provider + 4 module calls
├── outputs.tf                   <- ports, URLs, tunnel_command
├── terraform.tfvars.example     <- copy to terraform.tfvars, fill in values
├── README.md                    <- init/plan/apply commands
└── modules/
    ├── network/                 <- the private bridge network (lab_net)
    │   └── versions.tf  main.tf  outputs.tf
    ├── traefik/                 <- Traefik container (file provider, no Docker socket)
    │   └── versions.tf  variables.tf  main.tf  outputs.tf
    ├── web/                     <- Apache container (init = true for the self-heal demo)
    │   └── versions.tf  variables.tf  main.tf  outputs.tf
    └── monitoring/              <- Prometheus + Grafana (Loki and Promtail join in Step F)
        └── versions.tf  variables.tf  main.tf  outputs.tf

docs.title: README.md
docs.text:
Bob also writes a README.md inside infra/terraform/, documenting the layer end to end:

  • Layout: the file tree above, with the purpose of each file and module.
  • Quick start: the exact run order, fill in terraform.tfvars, run the Ansible bootstrap first, then init, plan, apply, and open the SSH tunnels.
  • Expected plan: what the first terraform plan should report, so you know a healthy run when you see one.
  • Idempotency: why a second plan must show no changes, and which lifecycle block makes that true.
  • Design decisions: the reasoning behind the file provider, init = true on Apache, and the loopback-only port bindings.
  • Tear-down: how to kill the tunnel and destroy the stack, with a warning that destroying removes the data volumes.

It doubles as a reference when you deploy in Module 2.

docs.title: What to check before moving on
docs.text:
WHY THE CONTRACT IS IN THE PROMPT

Left to itself, Bob picks reasonable but different names on every run: web instead of apache_web, admin instead of labadmin, traefik_remote_port instead of traefik_dashboard_url. Each one is fine in isolation and each one breaks a command in Module 2 or 3 that was written against the other name. Naming the contract up front is what makes the rest of the lab reproducible.

  • Every ports block sets ip = "127.0.0.1": this is the lab's entire security model (rule b)
  • A versions.tf declaring kreuzwerker/docker exists in the root and in every module, otherwise terraform init fails in Module 2 (rule a)
  • Every container has lifecycle { ignore_changes = [log_opts, user, working_dir, command] }, otherwise every future terraform plan shows phantom drift (rule c)
  • Traefik uses the file provider rather than docker auto-discovery (rule d)
  • The web container sets init = true; Module 3's self-healing demo is impossible without it (rule e)
  • Secrets appear only as variable references (var.grafana_admin_password), never literal values, and terraform.tfvars.example covers all inputs
  • The contract holds: containers are named traefik, apache_web, prometheus, grafana; grafana_admin_user defaults to labadmin; outputs.tf declares app_url, traefik_dashboard_url, grafana_url, prometheus_url, grafana_admin_user, tunnel_command. Module 2 calls every one of those by name

docs.title: iv. STEP C: GENERATE THE ANSIBLE LAYER
docs.text:
Now for the other half. Ansible handles everything Terraform does not: preparing the host itself (installing headless Rancher Desktop) and generating the content the containers serve. That content comprises the landing page, the Traefik routes, the Prometheus scrape config, and the Grafana dashboard.

  1. Copy and paste the contents of the following code block into the Agentic Sidebar, then hit Enter to eexecute. Since it is long, Bob may show it as a collapsed window — click the "copy" icon next to the text block to ensure you've captured the entire statement. Bob stays in Agent mode from Step B.

    Generate an Ansible layout under infra/ansible/ with an inventory file inventory.ini (using ansible_port, ansible_user and ansible_ssh_private_key_file so any non-default SSH port is supported), a top-level site.yml and roles:

In inventory.ini, write ansible_ssh_private_key_file as an absolute path and wrap the value in double quotes. INI inventory splits host lines on whitespace, so an unquoted path containing a space (a lab folder named "IBM BOB DEV OPS") fails to parse; Ansible then falls back to implicit localhost and silently runs every task against the operator's laptop instead of the server. A relative path breaks the same way whenever a command runs from a directory other than infra/ansible. Also set private_key_file in ansible.cfg as a fallback.

- common (kernel sysctls, journald limits - leave ufw alone, no public ports are used)
- docker (install headless Rancher Desktop if not present — the standalone rdd daemon binary from the rancher-desktop-2 GitHub releases, pinned to an exact release tag (v2.0.0-alpha.1 at time of writing) and never "latest": rdd is alpha and has no upgrade path between versions, so an unpinned install breaks this lab the day the next alpha ships. NOT the Rancher Desktop GUI app and NOT the rancher/rancher server image, neither of which runs on a headless SSH-only host. Run it as a systemd service so the engine survives reboots and SSH disconnects, and expose its Docker-compatible socket at the standard /var/run/docker.sock path so the Terraform provider and every docker command in this lab work unchanged — rdd's socket path is not documented, so discover it at runtime and then symlink it to /var/run/docker.sock rather than hardcoding a guess. rdd runs the Moby engine inside a Lima VM, so the host filesystem is NOT the daemon's filesystem: add /opt/lab to rdd's VM mount list as a writable mount before any container starts, and verify from inside Rancher Desktop that a file Ansible rendered on the host is actually readable there. Do not assume the bind mount resolved. Add the SSH user to the docker group only if the socket turns out to need it, set log driver = json-file with rotation, and configure a daily prune timer, noting in the README if rdd's engine does not support either)
- web_content (render the Apache vhost and landing page from Jinja templates into a host bind-mount)
- monitoring_content (Prometheus scrape config, Grafana datasource provisioning and a starter dashboard JSON)

Every task must be idempotent and tagged. Use an ansible-vault-friendly variable layout with group_vars/all/vars.yml and group_vars/all/vault.yml. Provide an ansible-lint-clean output and a one-liner to run the full playbook.

Terraform mounts these exact host directories, so create them and render into them with no extra nesting:
- /opt/lab/traefik/dynamic/routes.yml   one router matching PathPrefix(`/`) on the web entrypoint, service http://apache_web:80. No Host() rule: the operator arrives through a tunnel as localhost, which no Host rule matches.
- /opt/lab/web/index.html               the landing page. Its text must contain the word "Welcome", which Part 2 greps for.
- /opt/lab/prometheus/prometheus.yml    the scrape config
- /opt/lab/grafana/provisioning/        datasource and dashboard-provider files
- /opt/lab/grafana/dashboards/          the dashboard JSON

Every task that renders a file must be preceded by a task that creates its parent directory with state: directory. This applies to system paths too, not just /opt/lab: /etc/systemd/journald.conf.d does not exist on a fresh Ubuntu 22.04, so templating into it fails the play outright. Create system directories as standalone file tasks, not by adding them to the /opt/lab loop, so the bootstrap and content tag split stays clean.

Create every one of those directories mode 0755 and every rendered file mode 0644. The containers run as non-root (Prometheus as nobody, uid 65534), so a directory created 0750 root:root cannot be traversed by the process that has to read the file inside it, and Prometheus crash-loops with "open /etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml: permission denied" while the file itself looks perfectly readable.

Prefix every variable a role defines with that role's name — everything in defaults/, everything in vars/, and every register: (monitoring_content_result, not result; web_content_lab_root, not lab_root). ansible-lint's var-naming[no-role-prefix] applies to all three locations, not just register, and every unprefixed one is a separate failure that stops the Part 2 pre-flight before it deploys anything.

Start every task and handler name with a capital letter, or ansible-lint fails name[casing] once per task. If you prefix names with the role, capitalise the prefix too (Docker | Install prerequisites, not docker | Install prerequisites).

Tag every task in common and docker with `bootstrap` and every task in web_content and monitoring_content with `content`, because Part 2 invokes the playbook by those two tag names and nothing else. If the engine's socket does require group membership, put a meta: reset_connection immediately after the task that adds the SSH user to that group, or the rest of the run keeps the old membership and every docker call fails on the socket. Prove the bootstrap actually worked by running a plain `docker ps` over SSH at the end of the role, not by trusting that the playbook exited zero.

Write the dashboard JSON in Grafana's file-provisioning format: title, uid and schemaVersion at the top level, every panel with gridPos, every target with refId. Do not wrap it in a {"dashboard": {...}} envelope, which is the HTTP API format and makes Grafana reject the file with "Dashboard title cannot be empty" and show no dashboards at all. Only query metrics that a scrape target in prometheus.yml actually exports; Traefik and Prometheus itself are the only exporters here, so container and host metrics do not exist and any panel using them renders "No data".

Prometheus and Grafana read their config only at startup, and Terraform may have created them before these files existed, so give each a handler that restarts the container when its config changes and that does nothing when the container is not there yet.

Leave vault.yml unencrypted and gitignored, and do not set vault_password_file in ansible.cfg. Document the ansible-vault encrypt command in the README as the production step instead. Part 2 runs the playbook non-interactively, so a configured vault password file that does not exist fails every play before it starts.

Three details in the observability config that are wrong by default and silently break every dashboard built on them:

1. In the Prometheus scrape config, do not attach a static `service` label to any job whose target exports its own `service` label. Prometheus renames the exporter's label to `exported_service` and keeps the static one, so every query filtering on `service` matches nothing while the data sits under a different name. Set `honor_labels: true` on the Traefik job.
2. In the Traefik static config, the `metrics.prometheus` block must set `addRoutersLabels: true`, `addEntryPointsLabels: true` and `addServicesLabels: true`. Router-level metrics are off by default, so `traefik_router_*` does not exist unless you ask for it.
3. Any log scraper must label every stream with `container_name`, so a panel or pipeline stage can select one container. A single shared `job` label makes every container indistinguishable downstream.

docs.title: Bob's plan
docs.text:
1. Before writing anything, Bob works out where the two layers meet: the host paths that Terraform's containers mount and that Ansible must therefore populate.

    Host path What Ansible renders into it /opt/lab/traefik/dynamic/ Traefik's file-provider routes /opt/lab/web/ the Apache document root /opt/lab/prometheus/prometheus.yml the scrape config /opt/lab/grafana/provisioning/ the Grafana datasource and dashboards

  1. Bob then proposes a todo list and asks you to approve it. It covers the layout, the config files, the four roles, and two self-checks. Read the list first. It is Bob's plan for the whole step, and every item on it is explained further down, at the point where Bob runs it.

    Your list may include an extra item that Bob added on its own. In this run, Bob re-read the Step B files, found a bug in how a Terraform flag was written, and added the fix to the list. Bob always explains why it added something. Read that explanation, because work you did not ask for is the work most worth checking.

docs.title: Ansible generation
docs.text:
1. Bob announces it will write the entire Ansible layout in parallel batches. Approve the todo update.

  1. Approve again as Bob writes the files. It writes the config first (ansible.cfg, inventory.ini, group_vars, site.yml), then all four roles simultaneously, then the Jinja templates. It finishes with the Grafana dashboard JSON, the most complex artifact. This one approval covers eight of the todo items:

    SUB-TASK OBJECTIVES Sub-Task 1 Write ansible.cfg: which inventory to use and how to SSH to the host Sub-Task 2 Write inventory.ini with ansible_port, ansible_user, and the key file, so the non-standard SSH port works Sub-Task 3 Split group_vars/all/vars.yml from vault.yml so secrets can be encrypted later on their own Sub-Task 4 Write site.yml, tagged so Module 2 can run bootstrap and content rendering separately Sub-Task 5 Build the common role: kernel parameters and journal log limits Sub-Task 6 Build the docker role: install Rancher Desktop headless under systemd, expose its socket at /var/run/docker.sock, mount /opt/lab into the Rancher Desktop VM, log rotation, and a daily prune timer Sub-Task 7 Build the web_content role: Traefik's file-provider routes and the Apache landing page Sub-Task 8 Build the monitoring_content role: the Prometheus scrape config and the Grafana provisioning chain

    Bob works outward from the smallest dependency. Sub-tasks 1 to 4 come first because everything else refers to them, since a role cannot resolve a variable group_vars has not declared. The four roles do not depend on each other, so Bob writes them in one parallel batch. The Grafana dashboard JSON comes last, being the largest and most error-prone file.

docs.title: Validation and fixes
docs.text:
With 23 files written, Bob checks its own work. This run turns into a real bug hunt, and it is worth following closely, because it shows what Bob does when a check fails.

  1. Bob writes a Python script with five static checks. Every YAML file must parse, and every task must carry tags. Every template variable must match a declared vars.yml key, every Jinja template must render, and the dashboard JSON must be valid once the Jinja markers are stripped. This is the todo's two verification items being executed. Approve it.

    VERIFY IDEMPOTENCY PATTERNS ON EVERY TASK

    Bob's self-check for the prompt's "every task must be idempotent" rule: creates: and stat guards that make a task a no-op when the work is already done.

    VERIFY ALL TASKS ARE TAGGED

    Self-check for the other prompt rule, so any slice of the playbook can be run on its own.

    IF THE SCRIPT FAILS ON A MISSING PARSER

    The script needs PyYAML. If it is not on your machine, Bob installs it, confirms the install, and retries on its own. Approve those commands and the run continues.

  1. The suite runs against every generated file.

    • If a check fails, Bob patches the file and runs the suite again. Sometimes it finds the fault was in its own test rather than in the file.
    • Approve each round. What matters is where it ends. Every file should pass, and if Bob dismisses a failure it should be able to say why.

  1. The todo list closes out with every item done, and a final listing confirms the finished tree.

docs.text:

  1. Expand infra/ansible to see the full layout.

docs.title: What to check before moving on
docs.text:
• inventory.ini sets ansible_port, ansible_user, and ansible_ssh_private_key_file. These tell Ansible how to SSH into the server; without them it assumes port 22 and fails to connect at all on a non-default port like TechZone's
  • All four roles are present: common, docker, web_content, monitoring_content
  • Every task is tagged and idempotent; Module 2 runs this playbook more than once, so a second run must change nothing
  • The two tags Module 2 uses actually exist: ansible-playbook site.yml --list-tasks --tags bootstrap and --tags content each list tasks rather than nothing
  • If the role adds the SSH user to a group for socket access, a meta: reset_connection follows immediately after it
  • /opt/lab is mounted into the Rancher Desktop VM and the role proves it: a file Ansible rendered on the host must be readable from inside Rancher Desktop. Without this every bind mount silently resolves to an empty directory, and the whole stack comes up "healthy" while serving nothing.
  • Secrets live in group_vars/all/vault.yml and that file is gitignored. It stays unencrypted for the lab, so Module 2 can run the playbook without a vault prompt
  • The docker role installs Rancher Desktop only if missing, pinned to an exact release tag, runs it as a systemd service, and ends by proving the engine works with a plain docker ps over SSH

docs.title: v. STEP D: SECURITY & SECRETS REVIEW
docs.text:
In Steps B and C, Bob wrote a lot of code quickly, and you are about to run it against a real server. Before that happens, this step turns Bob into its own reviewer: it re-reads everything it just generated, checking for the kinds of mistakes that can hurt in production. For example:

  • A password sitting in a file
  • A port accidentally open to the whole internet instead of loopback
  • A container running with more privileges than it needs

  1. Paste the prompt below into Bob's chat and send it. Bob stays in Agent mode.

    Audit the generated Terraform and Ansible for: secrets in code or state, any port bound to 0.0.0.0 instead of 127.0.0.1, weak Grafana defaults, container privilege escalation, exposed Docker socket without read-only mode, missing resource limits and missing log drivers. For each finding give severity (low/med/high), exploit scenario in one line and the minimal fix as a unified diff. Then propose a remote-state backend (S3+DynamoDB or equivalent) with state encryption and locking, and an ansible-vault strategy for the Grafana admin password.

Four things are already decided. List them as accepted risks with the reason and leave the code alone:
- The Traefik dashboard and API stay unauthenticated. Only the operator's own SSH tunnel reaches them, and a generated BasicAuth hash is a password nobody can type.
- There is no TLS. SSH is the encryption layer and every operator URL is plain http on localhost.
- State stays local. Write the backend as a proposal; do not add a backend block, because terraform init would then try to resolve it and Part 2 has no cloud credentials.
- vault.yml stays unencrypted and gitignored, because Part 2 runs the playbook non-interactively.

Do not rename anything Part 2 depends on: the container names, grafana_admin_user, the bootstrap and content tags, or the /opt/lab paths. If a fix genuinely needs one of those changed, raise it as a finding and stop rather than applying it. If you harden SSH host key checking, use StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new and never yes, because Part 2 runs unattended and yes turns a first connection into a prompt nobody answers.

docs.title: The audit
docs.text:
1. Bob re-reads everything it wrote in Steps B and C, then turns the audit into a todo list of findings ranked by severity. Approve it, then read the findings before you approve any fix. This table is the security lesson of the module:

    FINDING SEVERITY THE FIX F-01 grafana_admin_password written to terraform.tfstate in plaintext HIGH Mark the output sensitive = true; the real cure is the encrypted remote backend in F-04 F-02 vault.yml holds the secret unencrypted, so any git add -A commits it HIGH A gitignore entry, plus the documented ansible-vault encrypt command for production F-04 No remote state backend, so state is unencrypted, unlocked, and unshared HIGH The S3 + DynamoDB design, written up as documentation rather than applied F-05 StrictHostKeyChecking=no lets an impostor server intercept the SSH connection MED accept-new, which pins the key on first use and still never prompts F-06 Grafana's GF_SECURITY_* settings left at defaults MED Set the hardening environment variables explicitly F-07 No resource limits, so one runaway container can starve the host MED Memory and CPU limits on every container F-08 No log_driver block, so containers log without bounds if daemon.json is wrong MED Declare the log driver per container F-09 No no_log, so sensitive tasks print the password into playbook output MED no_log: true on the tasks handling grafana_admin_password F-10 No .gitignore for terraform.tfvars and *.pem LOW Ignore the real variable values and the SSH private key F-11 Promtail mounts docker.sock to discover containers LOW Mount it read-only and narrow the bind to what Promtail actually reads

    Bob ranks by severity rather than by file, so the list doubles as a priority order.

    THE THREE HIGHS ARE A SINGLE PROBLEM

    F-01, F-02 and F-09 are all the same Grafana password, leaking through three different channels:

    Finding Where it leaks F-01 Terraform state F-02 git history F-09 playbook output

    F-04 is what would contain the first of them in production, and it is the one finding you deliberately do not apply here.

    Now notice what is missing from the table: the Traefik dashboard.

    Left unconstrained, Bob rates api.insecure=true a HIGH and puts a BasicAuth middleware in front of it, generating the password hash itself. The dashboard then answers 401 for the rest of the lab, and nobody knows the credentials.

    The accepted-risks block in your prompt is what keeps it out of the findings. Bob still records its reasoning in the report either way.

  1. Approve the todo list. Bob applies the fixes file by file, then writes the remote state backend and the ansible-vault strategy doc the prompt asked for. Approve the todo updates as it goes.

  1. Afterwards, Bob produces a Security Audit report. Each finding comes with its severity, a one-line exploit scenario, and the exact diff applied, followed by the accepted risks it left alone. Click Open on the report card and read it end to end.

    In this run Bob applied every fix itself, so your job shifts from applying to verifying:

    1. Read each finding in the report and decide whether you agree it was a real problem and that the fix is right.
    2. Spot-check the diffs in the changed files, the same way you reviewed Steps B and C.
    3. Ask Bob to revert anything you disagree with, and re-run the audit prompt if you want a clean pass to confirm.

    The result of this step is what you deploy in Module 2: code that has already survived a security review before it ever touched the server.

docs.title: What to check before moving on
docs.text:
• Every finding has all three parts: severity, exploit scenario, and a concrete diff; a finding without a fix is not actionable
  • Every high-severity finding is applied.
  • The re-run of the audit prompt comes back clean (or only with findings you have consciously accepted)
  • The accepted risks survived the audit untouched: no BasicAuth middleware appeared in front of the Traefik dashboard, no TLS was added, no backend block was written, and vault.yml is still readable
  • Nothing from the platform contract was renamed. Run the contract check in Review & Approval below before you move on
  • Bob wrote the two extras as documentation only: the remote state backend with encryption and locking, and the ansible-vault strategy for the Grafana admin password

docs.title: vi. REVIEW & APPROVAL
docs.text:
Bob has now generated everything Module 2 will deploy. Before you approve it, verify the properties that matter. Each check below is a command you paste into the Bob IDE terminal, and each catches a specific mistake.

1. Every published port binds to loopback

Every line this prints must say 127.0.0.1. A single 0.0.0.0 means a service is exposed to the internet and the security model is broken.

grep -rn 'ip *=' infra/terraform --include='*.tf'

2. Five versions.tf files exist — the root plus one per module

A missing one means terraform init fails in Module 2, because Terraform looks for the non-existent hashicorp/docker provider instead of kreuzwerker/docker.

ls infra/terraform/versions.tf infra/terraform/modules/*/versions.tf

3. The Apache container sets init = true

Module 3's self-healing demo is impossible without it: httpd running as PID 1 cannot be killed from inside the container.

grep -n 'init' infra/terraform/modules/web/main.tf

4. No literal passwords in the code

Every line this prints must be a variable reference or declaration (var.grafana_admin_password), never an actual password value.

grep -rni 'password' infra/terraform --include='*.tf'

5. The container names Modules 2 and 3 hardcode

All four must print. A rename here breaks the self-healing demo, which addresses containers by name.

grep -rn 'name *= *"' infra/terraform/modules --include='*.tf' \
  | grep -E 'traefik|apache_web|prometheus|grafana'

6. The output names Module 2 reads back after apply

All six must print.

grep -n '^output' infra/terraform/outputs.tf

7. The two Ansible tags Module 2 invokes

Both must list tasks. A tag that matches nothing makes Module 2 skip that half of the deployment silently.

cd infra/ansible
ansible-playbook site.yml --list-tasks --tags bootstrap | tail -5
ansible-playbook site.yml --list-tasks --tags content | tail -5
cd ../..

8. The accepted risks are still accepted

The Traefik dashboard carries no BasicAuth, TLS is absent, no remote backend block exists, and vault.yml remains readable. The last command must not print $ANSIBLE_VAULT;1.1 — an encrypted vault file makes Module 2's non-interactive run fail before it starts.

grep -rn 'basicauth\|users *=\|tls\|acme' infra/terraform --include='*.tf'
grep -rn 'backend "' infra/terraform --include='*.tf'
head -1 infra/ansible/group_vars/all/vault.yml

9. The linters actually pass

Module 2's pre-flight runs both of these and stops the deployment if either fails, without fixing anything. Prove it here instead.

terraform fmt -check -recursive infra/terraform
cd infra/ansible && ansible-lint; cd ../..

Both must print nothing and exit 0. Run them yourself even if Bob's Step E report says the code is clean.

TROUBLESHOOTING: terraform fmt -check PRINTS A FILENAME

Cause — that file's = signs are misaligned. Nothing else.

Fix — reformat in place:

terraform fmt -recursive infra/terraform

This is whitespace only and cannot change what your infrastructure does.

Always use -recursive. Plain terraform fmt -check looks at the current directory only and never descends into modules/, so it can pass while a module is still unformatted.

TROUBLESHOOTING: ansible-lint REPORTS DOZENS OF FAILURES

Cause — two rules account for almost all of them:

  • var-naming[no-role-prefix] — a variable in defaults/, vars/ or register: without its role-name prefix
  • name[casing] — a task name not starting with a capital letter

Both are cosmetic, but each occurrence counts as its own failure, so a handful of naming choices becomes 60+ findings.

Fix — paste the output back to Bob and have it correct the names before you approve the step.

TROUBLESHOOTING: BOB'S STEP E REPORT SAYS CLEAN BUT THE LINTERS DISAGREE

Cause — Step E can be answered from Bob's model of what the linters would say rather than by running them. The report then reads clean while the real tools fail.

Fix — trust the commands above rather than the report. Show Bob the real output and have it fix what the tools actually found.

Then two things to read rather than grep:

  • The architecture document from Step A — does it still match what Steps B and C actually generated?
  • The audit findings from Step D — is every high-severity finding either fixed or something you consciously decided to accept?

If a check fails, tell Bob what you found and have it fix the code, then re-run the check.

docs.title: vii. KEY TAKEAWAYS
docs.text:
• A one-paragraph requirement, enhanced into a structured spec and answered in Plan mode, produces a reviewable design document before any code exists.
  • The prompts pin every decision Bob would otherwise ask about, and they name the contract (container names, outputs, tags, paths) that Modules 2 and 3 depend upon.
  • Terraform owns what exists on the server; Ansible owns how the host is prepared and what content the containers serve, and both layers must name the same paths.
  • Bob validates its own output with checks it wrote itself; read those commands before approving them, and run the linters yourself regardless.
  • The security audit is constrained by an accepted-risks block, which is what keeps the tunnel-only Traefik dashboard out of the findings.
  • Whatever passes the review checks here is exactly what Module 2 deploys.

Continue to Validation & Enhancement, where the same plan-review loop adds four more steps. An idempotency, lint, and drift audit comes first, followed by the observability stack (Loki + Promtail). A disaster-recovery runbook and a CI/CD pipeline complete the module.

docs.title: Validation and Enhancement
docs.text: MODULE 1 | DESIGN

docs.title: i. WHAT YOU WILL VALIDATE AND ADD
docs.text:
Christopher Bienko (AI Enablement GTM Product Manager) provides an overview of the Design - Validation and Enhancement module for the hands-on enablement. [1 min]

AI MATURITY CURVE

This chapter contains the clearest illustration in the entire course of why the developer stays in control. In Step F, Bob begins building deliverables you have not asked for yet. Approving them is reasonable; approving them knowingly is the discipline. That judgment call is the same one you practiced throughout Module 2 | Delegate, and no amount of autonomy between the gates removes it.

Module 1 | Architecture and Planning ended with an architecture, a Terraform layer, an Ansible layer, and a security review. In this second-half, you will define four more prompt-review cycles within the Bob IDE:

  • Step E — audit the code for idempotency, lint findings, and weak drift detection
  • Step F — extend the monitoring stack with Loki and Promtail
  • Step G — produce a disaster-recovery and rollback runbook
  • Step H — wire up a CI/CD pipeline and a matching local check target

As in previous section, everything happens in Bob IDE on your laptop. Nothing is deployed until the Module 2 | Deploy chapters.

docs.title: ii. STEP E: IDEMPOTENCY, LINT, AND DRIFT AUDIT
docs.text:
Before introducing any new functionality, ask Bob to verify that the existing codebase is both lint-clean and idempotent.

A lint-clean codebase passes static quality checks without errors or warnings, while an idempotent deployment produces no changes when run repeatedly. The first execution may apply required updates, but a second execution should result in a no-op with zero additional changes.

  1. Click the task prompt field to start a new task.

  1. Select Plan mode. This step starts as a review, so Plan mode is the right posture: Bob reads and analyzes first, and nothing can change until you explicitly allow it.

  1. Paste the prompt below and send it:

    Run a static review against terraform fmt, terraform validate, tflint, ansible-lint and yamllint. Execute each tool as a real shell command and work from its actual output — do not reason about what a linter would probably report, and do not record a finding you have not seen a tool print. Use terraform fmt -check -recursive and ansible-lint with no path filter so nothing is skipped. If a tool is not installed, say so explicitly and mark that linter NOT RUN rather than simulating it. Fix every finding inline, then re-run every tool and paste the final output showing zero remaining failures. Then walk through what terraform plan should report on a second run (must be no-op) and what ansible-playbook --check --diff should report (must be 0 changed). Highlight any resource where drift detection is weak (null_resource, local-exec, manually-created host files) and propose stronger alternatives.

Propose those alternatives, do not build them. A checksum-and-assert mechanism layered on top of the existing tasks reports `changed` on every run, which breaks the idempotency proof it was meant to protect.

Leave the platform contract alone: container names, grafana_admin_user, the bootstrap and content tags, the /opt/lab paths, and the accepted risks recorded in Step D. If a linter flags one of them, say so and move on.

Then audit the observability contract, which linters cannot check. Extract every metric name referenced in the Grafana dashboard JSON and confirm each one is exported by a target configured in prometheus.yml, accounting for exporter flags that gate whole metric families and for label collisions that rename an exporter's labels. Extract every label selector used in Loki panels and confirm the log scraper's relabel config actually produces those labels. Report any panel whose query cannot resolve against the deployed configuration as a defect, with the specific config change that fixes it. A dashboard that renders "No data" on a healthy stack is a bug, not an empty state.

docs.title: Bob's plan
docs.text:
1. Bob finds real defects and needs write access to fix them, so it asks to switch to Agent mode. Approve the Switch mode to agent card. Plan mode kept Bob read-only until it could justify more, and the switch happens with your consent.

  1. Now in Agent mode, Bob lays out its findings as a todo list: one umbrella item, ten specific defects with locations, the three linter configs to write, and the idempotency doc.

    FINDING THE FIX TF-LINT-01 ssh_private_key_path has no validation block Validate the input so a bad path fails at plan time rather than apply time ANSIBLE-LINT-01/02 Jinja2 expressions and a stale StrictHostKeyChecking value in ansible.cfg Drop the Jinja2 (invalid in an INI file) and align the value with accept-new ANSIBLE-LINT-03 explicit no_log: false on docker role tasks Remove the unnecessary explicit false ANSIBLE-LINT-04 unquoted scrape_interval in prometheus.yml.j2 Quote it so YAML cannot parse it as the wrong type TF-FMT-01 non-canonical formatting across the .tf files Re-format 191 alignment-padded assignments to canonical style

    BOB CAUGHT ITS OWN ERROR

    Those 191 misformatted lines came from Bob in Step B. It only found them by re-checking work it had already called done.

    YOUR FINDINGS MAY DIFFER

    This table is one recorded run. What must not appear is a finding that undoes the platform contract or one of the accepted risks. That would mean a renamed container, a changed Grafana user, a BasicAuth middleware, a backend block, or StrictHostKeyChecking=yes. If one shows up, reject it here rather than discovering it during the Module 2 deployment.

  1. Approve the todo list.

docs.title: Validation commands
docs.text:
Bob now runs each linter in turn and works from what the tools actually report. Approve each command as it comes.

  1. Click Approve once for terraform validate, then ansible-lint and yamllint. These produce the TF-LINT and ANSIBLE-LINT findings in the table above.

  1. Then Approve once for terraform fmt, which is where TF-FMT-01 gets its number.

    IF BOB SIMULATES A LINTER INSTEAD OF RUNNING IT

    When a tool is missing from the laptop, Bob may write a Python script that approximates it rather than saying so. A simulated pass is worse than no pass: the report reads clean while the real tool would fail, and you find out mid-deployment in Module 2.

    Check that Bob names the actual command it ran. If it simulated one, install the missing tool and have it re-run for real.

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text:
1. The analysis finishes with 191 formatting findings, plus a handful of validate and lint issues.

    • Bob turns the results into a fix plan, with each item naming the exact change it will make. Approve it.
    • Almost all of the 191 come from one habit: the formatter Bob used in Step B lined up = signs across rows, and canonical terraform fmt style does not do that.

  1. Bob then proposes a Python rewriter that applies canonical single-space = formatting to every .tf file. Approve.

  1. If Step D left a stray backend.tf behind, Bob removes it here: the root versions.tf already owns the only terraform {} block, and a second one makes terraform init fail. Approve.

  1. After fixing the Ansible issues and writing the three linter configs, Bob runs the final comprehensive clean-state check. This one trips the security warning (a long chained command), so check I understand the risk, then approve.

    THE THREE LINTER CONFIGS: .YAMLLINT, .ANSIBLE-LINT, .TFLINT.HCL

    None of these existed before this step. Bob writes all three so the same checks run reproducibly, locally and later in CI (Step H), instead of living only inside this conversation.

  1. The Terraform half of that check fails, so Bob splits the work and runs the Ansible clean-state validation on its own. Approve.

  1. Ansible comes back clean (0 issues). The remaining formatting findings are all in variables.tf, where the new validation blocks re-introduced alignment; Bob re-applies the formatter to that one file. Approve.

  1. Bob re-checks the remaining findings before fixing them, and confirms some need no change. Inside required_providers, aligned source and version keys are canonical terraform fmt style, because same-length keys in one block stay aligned. Approve.

    Expect steps like this. Bob confirms a finding is real before editing code to satisfy it.

  1. All Terraform files are clean. Approve the todo update.

  1. Bob writes infra/IDEMPOTENCY.md and closes out the last todo item. Approve.

THE IDEMPOTENCY WALKTHROUGH AND DRIFT AUDIT DOC

This file delivers the second half of the prompt: proof of the second-run behavior (what terraform plan and ansible-playbook --check must report) and a catalogue of the places where drift detection is weak.

TROUBLESHOOTING: TASK LIMIT REACHED

Long runs like this one can hit the task's 100-turn maximum mid-flight. Bob pauses and shows a Task limit reached banner. Click Continue Task to double the limit for this task only, and Bob picks up exactly where it stopped.

docs.text:
1. Bob finishes with a Lint Review report artifact. Click Open to read it.

  1. The report opens in your browser with the headline numbers: 191 fmt issues, 5 validate/tflint, 5 ansible-lint, 0 remaining, 7 new config files. Below the stats, every finding gets an ID (TF-FMT-01, TF-VAL-01, ...), an explanation, the before/after diff, and a FIXED badge. This is the same evidence-per-finding shape as Step D's security report, applied to code quality.

  1. Back in Bob IDE, expand infra in the explorer. Two new files sit next to ansible/ and terraform/: gitignore.template from Step D, and IDEMPOTENCY.md.

    Bob's closing summary sets out what a second run must produce:

    Command Required result terraform plan -detailed-exitcode exits 0 ansible-playbook --check --diff reports changed=0

    It also lists 4 blind spots, places a clean terraform plan cannot actually vouch for, such as a file edited by hand under /opt/lab. Bob documents them instead of fixing them, because a check that catches them would report changed on every run and break the idempotency proof itself.

  1. Open infra/IDEMPOTENCY.md and review it: the exact commands to verify a clean second run, a table explaining why each Terraform resource is a no-op on a second plan, and the drift weaknesses with ready-to-paste fixes. Module 2 uses those verification commands for real.

    IF YOUR TERRAFORM PLAN IS NOT A NO-OP

    Check the lifecycle { ignore_changes = ... } blocks from Step B in Architecture & Planning. Without them, Rancher's log-opts and image defaults show up as diffs on every plan.

docs.title: Before moving on
docs.text:
WHY THIS MATTERS FOR MODULE 2

Deployment in Module 2 runs the playbook and terraform apply more than once. Idempotency is what makes those repeated runs safe rather than destructive.

First, run the linters yourself. Do not take Bob's report on trust: it can be written from Bob's idea of what the tools would say rather than from running them.

terraform fmt -check -recursive infra/terraform
cd infra/ansible && ansible-lint; cd ../..

Both must print nothing and exit 0. If Bob's report said the code was clean and ansible-lint now prints 63 findings, the review was simulated. Hand Bob the real output and have it fix them before you move on, or every one of those findings stops your deployment in Module 2.

Then check three things in what Bob produced:

  • Bob concludes a second terraform plan would be a no-op
  • Bob concludes ansible-playbook --check --diff would report changed=0
  • Any null_resource, local-exec, or hand-created file on the host is either gone, or Bob has said in writing why its drift risk is acceptable

docs.title: iii. STEP F: ADD THE OBSERVABILITY STACK
docs.text:
You cannot operate what you cannot see. Part 1 already gave you Prometheus and Grafana; this step adds the log side: Loki for aggregation and Promtail as the container logs scraper, turning the demo into a platform you can genuinely operate.

  1. Paste the following prompt (Bob stays in Agent mode) and hit Enter to execute:

    Extend the monitoring Terraform module and the monitoring_content Ansible role to add Loki for log aggregation and Promtail as a Docker logs scraper. Ansible renders /opt/lab/loki/loki-config.yml and /opt/lab/promtail/promtail-config.yml, and Terraform bind-mounts the parent directories /opt/lab/loki to /etc/loki and /opt/lab/promtail to /etc/promtail, read-only. Mount the directories, never the files. Configure Promtail so every log stream carries a container_name label; a shared job label alone makes containers indistinguishable and forces JSON parsing onto containers that do not emit JSON.

In the Loki compactor config, if you set retention_enabled: true you must also set delete_request_store: filesystem. Loki 3.x refuses to start without it and crash-loops with "CONFIG ERROR: invalid compactor config: compactor.delete-request-store should be configured when retention is enabled". Either set both or set neither.

Extend the dashboard Step C already created, in place, with the same filename, uid and title. The stack must end with exactly one provisioned dashboard, because Grafana's dashboard provider loads every file in the directory and a second one appears as a duplicate. Do not write a new dashboard file. It shows: Traefik request rate and 5xx ratio, Apache request rate, and a Loki panel with the last 100 Traefik access log lines. Make Grafana persist its DB on a named volume. Update outputs to expose grafana_url, prometheus_url and loki_url.

Before writing the dashboard, list the metric names each panel needs and confirm every one is actually exported by a configured scrape target. Do not emit a panel querying a metric you have not verified exists. If a panel would need an exporter this stack does not run, either add that exporter and its scrape job or leave the panel out, and say which you chose and why. Ratio panels must wrap the numerator in `or vector(0)` so they render 0 rather than "No data" when the numerator matches no series. The Loki panel must select by container_name so it reads one container's logs, and must filter out that container's own application log lines so only access log entries remain.

Every healthcheck you write must use a binary that actually exists in that container's image. The grafana/promtail image has no wget and no curl, so a wget-based test fails forever on a working container and Docker reports it unhealthy. Verify the binary is present before using it, and if the image ships no HTTP client, use a check that depends only on what is there.

docs.title: Bob's plan
docs.text:
1. Bob turns the prompt into a file-by-file todo list spanning both layers. Read it top to bottom; it is a precise map of everything one feature touches:

    SUB-TASK OBJECTIVES Sub-Task 1 Add the Loki and Promtail containers, images, and volumes to modules/monitoring/main.tf Sub-Task 2 Declare the new variables in the module and root variables.tf Sub-Task 3 Add the loki_url and container name outputs Sub-Task 4 Wire the new module arguments into the root main.tf Sub-Task 5 Document the new variables in terraform.tfvars.example Sub-Task 6 Write loki-config.yml.j2 and promtail-config.yml.j2 Sub-Task 7 Turn the datasource template into a multi-datasource file so Grafana reads Prometheus and Loki Sub-Task 8 Replace the dashboard JSON with the expanded version Sub-Task 9 Add the new Loki and Promtail keys to vars.yml Sub-Task 10 Add a Restart grafana handler so provisioning changes take effect Sub-Task 11 Validate the dashboard JSON after stripping the Jinja2 markers

    • Sub-task 11 is the one Bob added on its own: the JSON validation lesson from Step C, now a standing item it applies without being asked.

  1. Approve the todo list. Bob works through the Terraform layer first, then writes all the Ansible additions in parallel.

  1. The dashboard file is a Jinja template, so it is not valid JSON as written. Bob has to prove that what Ansible eventually renders will parse, because Grafana rejects a malformed dashboard outright and shows you none at all. It strips the Jinja markers, parses the result, and reports. Approve.

  1. The monitoring module gained new variables in this step, so Bob re-runs the mismatch check from Step B: every argument the root main.tf passes into a module must be one that module declares. Approve.

docs.title: Bob starts work you have not asked for yet
docs.text:
1. Read the next todo update before approving it. Alongside the observability items you asked for, Bob queues Makefile, tunnel.sh, RUNBOOK.md, .github/workflows/ci.yml, and a final end-to-end validation.

    • RUNBOOK.md belongs to Step G and the CI workflow belongs to Step H. Bob has worked out where the lab is heading and started building it early.
    • None of it was in your prompt. It comes from Bob's own Step A plan: this module has been one continuous session, so Bob can see which planned deliverables are still missing and has decided to finish them.
    • Approving is reasonable (but it's healthy to remain skeptical and critical). Trust, but verify.

  1. Bob re-reads the codebase so it has the complete picture, then asks to start on the expanded list. Approving here is what green-lights the extra work, and Bob executes the remaining tasks in parallel where possible.

  1. The Makefile lands first, then Bob writes tunnel.sh, the RUNBOOK, and the GitHub Actions CI pipeline in parallel. Watch the explorer fill in as each file is written.

  1. Approve the todo update recording the new files: .github/, Makefile, RUNBOOK.md, and tunnel.sh are now all in the tree.

docs.title: Final validation
docs.text:
1. Bob finishes with an end-to-end validation suite over the whole repository, seventeen checks run as shell commands. The first batch confirms that 0.0.0.0 bindings are absent everywhere, that :latest image tags are absent, and that 127.0.0.1 appears on every ports block. Approve.

  1. The suite continues (tunnel.sh has a valid shebang, Ansible modules use fully qualified names, the loki/promtail variables made it into terraform.tfvars.example). This batch trips the security warning, so check I understand the risk and approve. One check comes back as a false alarm and Bob says so: the 0.0.0.0 match is inside a README documentation comment rather than in any resource.

  1. The structural checks close it out. They confirm the CI workflow's jobs, the RUNBOOK's section count, and the Makefile's targets. They also confirm that no secret values leaked into terraform.tfvars.example and that tunnel.sh was made executable. Approve.

  1. All checks pass. Approve the final todo update; everything is complete.

  1. Read Bob's completion summary before moving on. It names each new file with its purpose: the 21-target Makefile, tunnel.sh with background/kill/status flags, the 20-section disaster-recovery runbook, and the 4-job GitHub Actions pipeline.

    The final validation results sit underneath: 39 of 39 required files present, loopback-only bindings confirmed, latest tags absent, and fully qualified Ansible module names throughout.
