docs.title: iv. STEP G: DISASTER RECOVERY AND ROLLBACK
docs.text:
DevOps maturity is measured by how quickly you can recover. Before deploying anything, write down how you would rebuild, roll back, and restore it.

A runbook already exists; Bob wrote one during Step F's scope expansion. This step holds it to a specific standard: the four recovery paths that matter for this stack, with a one-page TL;DR on top. Rather than assuming the existing file is good enough, you give Bob the requirement and let it judge.

  1. Paste the following prompt and and hit Enter to execute. You can see the old runbook's 20-section table of contents in the editor as you execute it:

    Write the runbook to infra/RUNBOOK.md. If a runbook already exists elsewhere in the repo, move it there rather than leaving two copies. Produce a runbook covering: (1) full rebuild from scratch on a brand-new Ubuntu host (with RTO/RPO assumptions), (2) selective container rollback when a new image is bad, (3) Grafana and Prometheus volume backup and restore using docker run --rm -v and tar, (4) what terraform destroy will and will not remove and the manual cleanup steps. Output as a single RUNBOOK.md with a "if you only read one page" TL;DR at the top.

docs.title: Bob's response
docs.text:
1. Bob judges the existing runbook against the prompt and rewrites it from scratch rather than patching it. The new TL;DR appears in the editor: a table pairing each situation with its action and rough recovery time, with the RTO and RPO assumptions underneath.

  1. Bob then validates its own output, checking that every required section and topic is present. Approve the command.

  1. The validation passes and Bob walks you through the finished RUNBOOK.md, section by section, ending with the design decisions that make this runbook worth reading rather than mere documentation filler:

    • prometheus_data is safe to back up live (its TSDB write-ahead log is crash-consistent), but grafana_data and loki_data are not; their containers must be stopped first. Bob calls this out as the most common operator mistake.
    • keep_locally = true on images means terraform apply will not delete images during replacement, but terraform destroy still removes them.
    • Section 4.2 enumerates every piece of host state that Ansible owns and Terraform does not, with the exact rm and apt purge commands to remove each, which is exactly what "what will terraform destroy NOT remove" was asking for.
    • Open infra/RUNBOOK.md and read the TL;DR page. It is the page you will actually use as a reference guide.

docs.text:
A single infra/RUNBOOK.md, opening with the "If You Only Read One Page" TL;DR and structured as:

  1. Full rebuild from scratch, with the RTO/RPO assumptions table
  2. Selective container rollback for a bad image
  3. Volume backup and restore, one subsection per volume, plus archive verification
  4. What terraform destroy will and will not remove: what IS destroyed (7 containers, 3 volumes, 1 network, the images), what is NOT (12 items of host state), the safe destroy procedure, and full host wipe commands

docs.title: v. STEP H: CI/CD PIPELINE INTEGRATION
docs.text:
IaC (Infrastructure as Code) only delivers value when every change goes through review, plan, and gated apply. The final step of Module 1 wires the whole validation suite into a pipeline and mirrors it locally, so developers get the same pass/fail signal before pushing.

Like Step G, part of this already exists: Bob wrote a CI workflow (ci.yml) during Step F's scope expansion. The prompt states the full requirement anyway, and Bob reconciles what exists against what is asked.

  1. Paste the following prompt and hit Enter to execute:

    Generate a GitHub Actions workflow .github/workflows/iac.yml with three jobs: validate (fmt, validate, tflint, ansible-lint), plan (on PR, posts the terraform plan as a PR comment using a least-privilege token), and apply (on merge to main, requires environment approval). Add a matrix step that runs the playbook in --check --diff against a staging inventory. Add a make ci-local target that reproduces the same checks on a developer laptop.

docs.title: Bob's plan
docs.text:
1. Bob reads the repo before writing anything and spots a gap: the prompt asks for a staging run, but no staging inventory exists for it to run against. So it adds one.

    The todo list comes back with three deliverables:

    File What Bob does .github/workflows/iac.yml write the validate, plan and apply jobs infra/ansible/inventory.staging.ini create the missing staging inventory infra/Makefile add the ci-local target

    Approve the list.

docs.title: Generation and validation
docs.text:
1. Bob writes all three files at once, then asks to validate them. Its checks cover two things:

    • Does it work? The workflow YAML parses, all three jobs are there, the ci-local target resolves, and the staging inventory exists.
    • Is it safe? No secrets hardcoded in the workflow, every sensitive value passed through secrets.*.
    • This is a chained command, so it trips the security warning. Check I understand the risk and approve.

  1. Two checks flag something that looks wrong but is not, and Bob explains each rather than passing or failing it silently:

    • The secret-looking matches are comments and temporary /tmp paths rather than real credentials.
    • Triggers: [] looks like the workflow has no triggers. It is a known Python YAML quirk where on: is read as a boolean. Bob checks the trigger block separately and confirms it is fine.
    • Approve the final todo update.

docs.title: Workflow review
docs.text:
1. Click the .github folder in the explorer and read Bob's closing summary.

    • It covers the staging inventory, named so the matrix step resolves it automatically, and a table mapping each ci-* Makefile target to the CI step it reproduces.
    • One target sits outside ci-local: ci-ansible-check needs a live host, so it runs on its own and skips cleanly when the inventory and key are missing.

  1. Expand .github/workflows and you will find two workflow files, from two different moments in the lab:

    • ci.yml: the 4-job validation pipeline from Step F's scope expansion. It answers "is the code sound?" on every push.
    • iac.yml: this step's deployment workflow, with plan on pull requests and apply gated behind an environment approval. It answers "should this change ship, and did a human sign off?"

    The two workflows overlap where they both validate, so merging them is a reasonable follow-up prompt. The lab keeps them separate to show the two halves of CI/CD: continuous validation and gated delivery.

docs.title: What Bob generates
docs.text:
.github/workflows/iac.yml with the three requested jobs:

  1. validate, which also runs the playbook with --check --diff against the staging inventory.
  2. plan (posts the Terraform plan as a PR comment).
  3. apply (gated behind a GitHub environment approval) — plus read-only default token permissions and a concurrency group so runs on the same ref do not race.

An updated Makefile whose ci-local target chains the same checks the CI validate job runs, minus anything needing a live connection:

ci-local: ci-tf-fmt ci-tf-validate ci-ansible-lint ci-guard

Each stage is also a standalone target:

  • ci-tf-fmt: format check
  • ci-tf-validate: init without backend, validate root and modules, tflint
  • ci-ansible-lint: yamllint, ansible-lint, syntax check
  • ci-guard: greps for 0.0.0.0 bindings and latest image tags
  • ci-ansible-check: the live-host check, kept out of ci-local and skipped cleanly when no staging host is reachable

Because terraform init runs with -backend=false, ci-local needs no cloud credentials.

# same pass/fail signal as CI, on your laptop
make ci-local

apply IS DELIBERATELY EXCLUDED FROM ci-local

The Makefile has an apply target, but it is excluded from ci-local and asks for confirmation: applying is a change to the live environment and belongs behind the CI approval gate rather than in a local lint loop.

Check before approving:

  • Workflow jobs match the prompt: validate, plan (PR comment), apply (environment approval)
  • The playbook --check --diff step targets a staging inventory
  • The token is least-privilege (contents: read by default)
  • make ci-local runs the same checks in the same order as the CI validate job
