├── Makefile                        # Entry point for automation: lint, validate, plan, apply
├── .github/workflows/iac.yml       # CI pipeline: format, validate, tflint, ansible-lint
├── .tflint.hcl                     # Terraform linter configuration
└── infra/
    ├── RUNBOOK.md               # Operational and disaster-recovery procedures
    ├── ansible/
    │   ├── ansible.cfg             # Ansible behavior (inventory path, SSH settings)
    │   ├── inventory.ini           # The target server: IP, port, user, key
    │   ├── inventory.staging.ini   # Staging inventory used for --check dry runs
    │   ├── site.yml                # Main playbook — applies all roles in order
    │   ├── group_vars/all/
    │   │   ├── vars.yml            # Shared variables (versions, paths, ports)
    │   │   └── vault.yml           # Secrets, encrypted with Ansible Vault
    │   └── roles/
    │       ├── common/             # Base host setup
    │       ├── docker/             # Installs Rancher Desktop (pinned) + /opt/lab VM mount + prune timer
    │       ├── web_content/        # Renders Apache pages and Traefik routes
    │       └── monitoring_content/ # Renders Prometheus, Grafana, Loki configs
    └── terraform/
        ├── main.tf                 # Root module — wires the four modules together
        ├── variables.tf  outputs.tf  versions.tf
        ├── terraform.tfvars.example  # Template — copy to terraform.tfvars
        └── modules/
            ├── network/            # Private Docker network (lab_net)
            ├── traefik/            # Reverse proxy container
            ├── web/                # Apache container
            └── monitoring/         # Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, Promtail containers

In short: the Makefile is the entry point (make help lists every target), Terraform defines what exists on the server, Ansible configures it, and secrets stay encrypted in Ansible Vault.

Everything is reproducible, reviewable, and can be diffed in a pull request. And nothing has been deployed yet. That is what Module 2 is for.

docs.title: vii. KEY TAKEAWAYS
docs.text:
• Bob's own report is never the proof; run the linters yourself, and treat a simulated pass as worse than no pass.
  • Idempotency is what makes Module 2's repeated runs safe, and the lifecycle blocks from Step B are what keep terraform plan a no-op.
  • Adding Loki and Promtail is one feature walking the entire Terraform chain, from module to root to example file.
  • When Bob expands scope on its own, approve knowingly: you are the only check on scope.
  • A runbook is held to a standard of recovery paths and a one-page TL;DR, and Bob rewrites rather than patches when the existing file falls short.
  • CI/CD comes in two halves — continuous validation on every push, and gated delivery behind a human approval — mirrored locally by make ci-local.

Continue to Single-Prompt Deployment, where Bob Shell takes the code you just reviewed and deploys it to the real host — bootstrap, apply, tunnels, and validation.

docs.title: Automated Deployment
docs.text: MODULE 2 | DEPLOY

docs.title: i. WHAT YOU WILL DEPLOY
docs.text:
Christopher Bienko (AI Enablement GTM Product Manager) provides an overview of the Deploy - Automated Deployment module for the hands-on enablement. [1 min]

AI MATURITY CURVE

This module is delegation at its widest scope. A single prompt carries the entire deployment, and its constraints forbid Bob from editing the code that Module 1 already reviewed. Auto-approve stays off, so you gate the run at each step. The reach is far greater than anything in the previous course; the discipline is identical.

In this module you switch to Bob Shell and let one prompt deploy the whole platform onto the remote Ubuntu server.

Key idea: The remote host has no public web ports. Every container binds to 127.0.0.1 on the server. The operator reaches everything through SSH local-forward tunnels opened by Bob Shell, hitting http://localhost:<port> on the laptop.

docs.title: Confirm your environment variables are still set
docs.text:
Both pre-flight steps are terminal commands rather than prompts: run them in the Bob IDE terminal, the same one you used in Setup. Bob Shell only comes into play in the next section, when you paste the deployment prompt.

This module uses the same five environment variables you exported in Setup → Environment Configuration. Confirm they are still set:

echo "HOST=$TARGET_HOST  USER=$SSH_USER  PORT=$SSH_PORT  KEY=$SSH_KEY"
test -n "$TF_VAR_grafana_admin_password" && echo "grafana password: set" || echo "grafana password: MISSING"

Every value should print. If it does, continue to the next check.

TROUBLESHOOTING: A VALUE PRINTS BLANK OR MISSING

Environment variables only exist inside the shell session that exported them. If you closed the terminal or Bob IDE since Setup, or are starting Part 2 on another day, they are gone. Re-export them before continuing:

export TARGET_HOST=[paste public IP here]
export SSH_USER=[paste SSH username here]
export SSH_PORT=[paste SSH port here]
export SSH_KEY=[paste path to SSH key file here]
export TF_VAR_grafana_admin_password='[type the same Grafana password as in Setup]'

As a reminder of where each value lives:

  • TARGET_HOST, SSH_USER, SSH_PORT: on your TechZone reservation page (My reservations → your reservation)
  • SSH_KEY: the path to the .pem file you downloaded into the lab folder
  • TF_VAR_grafana_admin_password: use the same password as in Setup. If the platform was already deployed once with a different password, Grafana keeps the old one and your login fails later.

docs.title: Confirm you're in the right place
docs.text:
Paste this block into the Bob IDE terminal:

pwd
ls infra/
terraform -version
ansible --version
ssh -i "$SSH_KEY" -p $SSH_PORT -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=5 ${SSH_USER}@${TARGET_HOST} 'sudo -n true && echo sudo-ok'

Check the output of each command:

  • pwd: prints your lab folder, the project root from Module 1
  • ls infra/: lists the two directories Bob generated, ansible and terraform
  • terraform -version and ansible --version: each prints a version number
  • the ssh command: prints sudo-ok, which proves you can reach the server and run sudo without a password

If all of that checks out, you are ready to deploy. If the last command does not print sudo-ok, return to Setup and fix the SSH connection first.

docs.title: Clear pre-existing host breakage
docs.text:
TechZone Ubuntu images frequently arrive with a half-configured shim-signed package. Its post-install script tries to mount an EFI partition that does not exist on a cloud VM, so it fails on every apt operation. Ansible then cannot install the packages Rancher Desktop needs, its service never starts, and you end up debugging two failures that look like one.

Thirty seconds spent now avoids all of it. Run this before you deploy:

ssh -i "$SSH_KEY" -p $SSH_PORT ${SSH_USER}@${TARGET_HOST} '
  sudo dpkg --configure -a
  sudo apt-get install -f -y
  sudo dpkg --audit
  echo "dpkg state: clean"
'

NEVER REMOVE shim-signed

It is a protected, boot-critical package and dpkg refuses to remove it. It is also entirely unrelated to Rancher Desktop. dpkg --configure -a completes its configuration and clears the error state, and that alone is the fix.

You need not check for Rancher Desktop on the server. Ansible installs it in the next section if it is missing.

dpkg --audit printing nothing before dpkg state: clean means the package manager is healthy and the deployment will run straight through. This is idempotent — on a host that was already fine it changes nothing.

docs.title: Create terraform.tfvars
docs.text:
Module 1 generated infra/terraform/terraform.tfvars.example, a template rather than the real file. Terraform needs the real one. Four variables have no default (target_host, ssh_user, ssh_private_key_path, domain), and ssh_port defaults to 22 rather than your TechZone port.

Your TARGET_HOST and SSH_USER exports do not help here: Terraform reads only environment variables prefixed TF_VAR_, which is why TF_VAR_grafana_admin_password is the one that works without a file. Without this step, terraform apply stops to prompt for four values and the non-interactive Bob Shell run fails partway through.

Paste this in the Bob IDE terminal, from the lab folder:

cat > infra/terraform/terraform.tfvars <<EOF
target_host          = "$TARGET_HOST"
ssh_user             = "$SSH_USER"
ssh_port             = $SSH_PORT
ssh_private_key_path = "$(cd "$(dirname "$SSH_KEY")" && pwd)/$(basename "$SSH_KEY")"
domain               = "localhost"
grafana_admin_user   = "labadmin"
EOF
cat infra/terraform/terraform.tfvars

terraform.tfvars IS SECRET-ADJACENT — NEVER COMMIT IT

It carries your server address, SSH user and key path. Module 1 Step D generated a gitignore template covering it; confirm terraform.tfvars is listed there before any git add.

Read back what it printed. Three things must be right:

  • grafana_admin_password is absent. It stays in TF_VAR_grafana_admin_password so your password never lands on disk. Do not add it here.
  • ssh_private_key_path is absolute. Terraform runs from infra/terraform/, so a relative ./key.pem resolves to the wrong place and the provider cannot reach the Rancher socket on the remote host.
  • domain is localhost. You arrive through an SSH tunnel as localhost, and a real domain in a Traefik Host() rule matches nothing — you would get a 404 from a stack whose containers all look healthy.

docs.title: iii. OPENING BOB SHELL
docs.text:
1. In the Bob IDE terminal where you just ran the pre-flight (the same session, so Bob Shell inherits your five environment variables), type bob and press Enter:

  1. The Bob Shell banner appears and the input field at the bottom is ready for a prompt. Before continuing, glance at two things: the path under the banner should be your lab folder, and the status bar at the bottom shows the mode and token meter you will watch during the run.

docs.title: iv. THE DEPLOYMENT PROMPT
docs.text:
Use the prompt below exactly in Bob Shell. If your CLI supports context attachment, attach the inventory using @infra/ansible/inventory.ini. There is neither a make deploy target nor a wrapper script; the prompt itself performs the deployment.

LAUNCH BOB SHELL FROM THE BOB IDE TERMINAL

Start Bob Shell in the same terminal session you just ran the pre-flight in, so it inherits your five environment variables. The prompt below references ${TARGET_HOST}, ${SSH_KEY} and the rest; in a fresh session those are empty and the run fails at the first step.

THE ${...} PLACEHOLDERS STAY UNEXPANDED, AND THAT IS EXPECTED

Exporting a variable makes it available to programs Bob runs. It does not rewrite text you paste. A shell only expands ${TARGET_HOST} when the shell itself reads the line, and pasting into Bob's input box is not that, so Bob receives the literal characters ${TARGET_HOST}.

That is why the first instruction in the prompt tells Bob to read the values out of its own environment. Without it, Bob sees a template full of blanks. It then stops halfway through the run to ask you for the host, the user, the port, and the key path.

The prompt pins everything down. It specifies which key and port every call must use, the exact steps in order, the hard constraints, and what to report back. That precision is what makes the run repeatable, and it is the run from which the expected output (below) was produced.

You are an agentic DevOps assistant operating inside this repository.

Goal: deploy and validate the full containerized web platform on a remote Ubuntu host that exposes ONLY SSH. All web access is via SSH local-forward tunnels from my laptop - no public ports are opened on the cloud side.

The ${...} placeholders below arrive as literal text, because pasting into a chat box does not expand shell variables. The values are exported in the environment you inherited, so read them yourself first and never ask me to re-type them:

    env | grep -E '^(TARGET_HOST|SSH_USER|SSH_PORT|SSH_KEY)='
    test -n "$TF_VAR_grafana_admin_password" && echo "grafana password: set" || echo "grafana password: MISSING"

That must print four lines plus "set". If anything is missing, stop and say which.

Context:
- Target host: ${TARGET_HOST}
- SSH user:    ${SSH_USER}
- SSH port:    ${SSH_PORT}
- SSH key:     ${SSH_KEY}    (already chmod 600)
- Terraform:   infra/terraform/
- Ansible:     infra/ansible/
- Inventory:   infra/ansible/inventory.ini

All ssh / scp / rsync calls MUST use `-i ${SSH_KEY} -p ${SSH_PORT}`.
All ansible calls MUST pass `--private-key "${SSH_KEY}"`, always double-quoted (do NOT rely on `ansible_ssh_private_key_file` in the inventory - relative paths there resolve from cwd, which breaks when ansible is invoked from the project root). Quote every path you interpolate: the lab folder may contain spaces, and an unquoted one splits into separate arguments, producing "no such identity: /Users/you/Documents/IBM".
The Terraform docker provider host MUST be `ssh://${SSH_USER}@${TARGET_HOST}:${SSH_PORT}` using the same key, with `IdentitiesOnly=yes` in `ssh_opts`. Either host-key posture is correct: `StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new` with a real `UserKnownHostsFile` (what Step D hardens it to) or `=no` with `/dev/null`. Never `=yes` — this run is unattended. Only report and stop if the host, port, user or key is wrong.

Required steps:

1) Pre-flight
   - `ssh -i ${SSH_KEY} -p ${SSH_PORT} ${SSH_USER}@${TARGET_HOST} 'sudo -n true'` must succeed.
   - Run `terraform fmt -check`, `terraform validate`, `ansible-lint`. Stop on any error.

2) Bootstrap (Ansible - host preparation)
   - cd infra/ansible
   - ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini site.yml --tags bootstrap
   - This must: install Rancher Desktop headless if missing, run it under systemd, expose its socket at /var/run/docker.sock, mount /opt/lab into the Rancher Desktop VM so bind mounts resolve, add ${SSH_USER} to the docker group if the socket needs it and refresh the SSH session group membership, configure log rotation.
   - Verify with: `ssh -i ${SSH_KEY} -p ${SSH_PORT} ${SSH_USER}@${TARGET_HOST} 'docker ps'`

3) Provision (Terraform)
   - cd infra/terraform
   - terraform init
   - terraform plan -out tfplan and summarise what will be created
   - terraform apply tfplan
   - Confirm every container `ports` block uses `ip = "127.0.0.1"`. Fail loudly if any is on 0.0.0.0.
   - Confirm every bind-mount source is an absolute directory under /opt/lab on the remote host. If one names a file (index.html, prometheus.yml) or uses path.module, stop and report it: Docker creates a missing file source as a directory of that name and the container dies with "not a directory". That is a Part 1 defect, not something to patch here.
   - Run `terraform output` and capture the values it prints; use those URLs in step 8 rather than re-typing them from this prompt.

4) Configure (Ansible - content)
   - cd infra/ansible
   - ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini site.yml --tags content
   - Re-run with `--check --diff` and confirm 0 changed (idempotency proof).

5) Open SSH tunnels (in the background, from this laptop)
   - Start a single multiplexed ssh session that forwards:
       8080 -> 127.0.0.1:80           (app via Traefik)
       8081 -> 127.0.0.1:8080         (Traefik dashboard)
       3000 -> 127.0.0.1:3000         (Grafana)
       9090 -> 127.0.0.1:9090         (Prometheus)
   - Command, writing the PID to /tmp/lab-tunnel.pid so step 8 can kill it:
       ssh -i ${SSH_KEY} -p ${SSH_PORT} -fN -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes \
           -L 8080:127.0.0.1:80 \
           -L 8081:127.0.0.1:8080 \
           -L 3000:127.0.0.1:3000 \
           -L 9090:127.0.0.1:9090 \
           ${SSH_USER}@${TARGET_HOST}
       pgrep -f "ssh.*-L 8080:127.0.0.1:80.*${TARGET_HOST}" > /tmp/lab-tunnel.pid
   - Wait up to 5 seconds for the forwards to be ready.

6) Validate (everything via localhost)
   - curl -fsS http://localhost:8080/             -> 200, body contains "Welcome"
   - curl -fsS http://localhost:8081/api/overview -> 200 (Traefik API)
   - curl -fsS http://localhost:3000/api/health   -> 200 (Grafana)
   - curl -fsS http://localhost:9090/-/healthy    -> 200 (Prometheus)
   - List the running containers on the remote host:
     `ssh -i ${SSH_KEY} -p ${SSH_PORT} ${SSH_USER}@${TARGET_HOST} \
         "docker ps --format '{{.Names}} {{.Status}} {{.Ports}}'"`
   - Confirm every published port is `127.0.0.1:<port>->...`, never `0.0.0.0:`.
   - Open Grafana's dashboard list via the API and confirm exactly one dashboard is provisioned, then query Prometheus for every metric its panels reference and report any that returns no series. A healthy container and an HTTP 200 do not prove a panel has data behind it.

7) Self-healing demo (60 seconds)
   IMPORTANT: do NOT use `docker stop` or `docker kill` from outside - Docker treats those as
   a deliberate user stop and `restart: always` will not fire. To prove real self-healing,
   crash the application process from INSIDE the container so the exit looks unexpected to
   the daemon. This requires `init = true` on the container (set in Part 1 Step B) so PID 1
   is `tini` and the application is PID 2+ - Linux protects PID 1 from SIGKILL inside its
   own PID namespace, so without tini, killing the in-container app from within is a no-op.

   - Capture before:  `ssh ... docker inspect apache_web -f '{{.State.StartedAt}} restartCount={{.RestartCount}}'`
   - Crash:           `ssh ... "docker exec apache_web sh -c 'kill -9 \$(pidof httpd | tr \" \" \"\\n\" | sort -n | head -1)'"`
   - Wait 8-12 seconds.
   - Capture after:   same inspect - `restartCount` must increment by 1 and `StartedAt` must be newer.
   - Re-curl http://localhost:8080/ - must return 200 again automatically.
   - Print the exact crash command you ran. If it contains `docker stop` or `docker kill`, the demo did not prove anything and you must report it as failed.

8) Print the operator URLs and how to tear down
   - Print:
       App        : http://localhost:8080
       Traefik UI : http://localhost:8081
       Grafana    : http://localhost:3000   (<grafana_admin_user> / <masked>)
       Prometheus : http://localhost:9090
   - Print the kill command for the tunnel:
       kill $(cat /tmp/lab-tunnel.pid)   # or: pkill -f 'ssh.*-L 8080:127.0.0.1:80'

Constraints:
- Do NOT modify Terraform or Ansible code; only run it. If something is broken, report the file, the defect and the fix, and stop.
- That no-edit rule covers the repository only, never the server. If the host arrives already broken - dpkg/apt failing to configure a pre-existing package, a systemd unit in a failed state, the rdd unit hitting its start limit - repairing the host is expected: fix it, state exactly what you ran and why, and continue.
- These are two separate host failures; fixing apt does not fix the second. If the rdd unit is in a failed state after a bad apt run, that is a start-limit rather than a package problem: run `systemctl reset-failed rdd.service`, then `systemctl start rdd.service`. There is no `docker.service` or `docker.socket` on this host - rdd is not socket-activated - so do not try to start them. Never remove or force-reinstall `shim-signed` - it is boot-critical, dpkg refuses it, and it is unrelated to the container engine.
- Do NOT place configuration on the host by hand. No scp of templates, no rendering files into /tmp, no editing anything under /opt/lab over ssh. Every file on that server must arrive through the Ansible playbook. If a play fails, report the failure and stop; a hand-placed file is invisible to `--check` and destroys the idempotency proof this lab exists to demonstrate.
- If the playbook appears to hang, do NOT work around it. Stop and check the inventory first: run `ansible-inventory --list` from infra/ansible. A parse failure there makes Ansible fall back to implicit localhost, and every subsequent task silently targets the laptop instead of the server.
- Never echo TF_VAR_grafana_admin_password to stdout; mask it.
- If any step fails, stop and print the failing command, the last 30 lines of output, and the proposed remediation.
- Never bind any container to 0.0.0.0. The whole point of this lab is the tunnel-only access model.
- A deliverable you cannot produce is a failure, not a skip. Never substitute a different proof for a missing one: a clean terraform plan says nothing about Ansible idempotency.

Deliverables:
- Summarised bootstrap / plan / apply / play log
- Final localhost URLs the operator can open in a browser
- Idempotency proof (Ansible second run = 0 changed, terraform plan = no changes)
- Self-healing proof (container down -> back up automatically)
- Tear-down command for the SSH tunnel

THE CONSTRAINTS ARE THE CONTRACT

The prompt never lets the agent edit code. Module 1 already generated and reviewed it; this prompt only runs it. If a step fails, the agent must stop and report rather than improvise a fix.

Pasted into Bob Shell, the input field grows to hold the whole prompt. Check the bottom bar before you hit Enter: Auto-approve Off (you gate the run) and the token meter showing plenty of headroom:

docs.title: What the prompt walks Bob through
docs.text:
The prompt walks Bob through eight phases:

  1. ssh-check the remote host (custom port, key auth, passwordless sudo)
  2. ansible-playbook to bootstrap the host (install Rancher Desktop if missing, grant socket access)
  3. terraform init / plan / apply against the remote Rancher socket over SSH
  4. ansible-playbook again for content (vhosts, dashboards, scrape configs)
  5. open the SSH tunnels for app/Traefik/Grafana/Prometheus
  6. curl every localhost:<port> and confirm 200 / healthchecks
  7. run a 60-second self-healing demo (kill a container, watch it come back)
  8. print the final localhost URLs the operator can open in a browser

The next section shows what that looks like when it runs.

docs.title: v. EXPECTED OUTPUT SHAPE
docs.text:
When Bob Shell finishes the prompt, it reports a Deployment Complete checklist shaped like this (with the exact wording and counts depending on your host and image tags):

Deployment Complete — Containerized Web Platform

Summary
Successfully deployed and validated the full containerized web platform
on the remote host with tunnel-only access (no public ports).

Deployment Steps Completed

1. Pre-flight Checks ✓
   - SSH sudo access confirmed
   - Terraform fmt/validate passed
   - Ansible-lint passed (warnings non-blocking)

2. Bootstrap ✓
   - Container engine present on the host (Rancher Desktop, installed via Ansible when missing)

3. Terraform Provision ✓
   - Plan applied, all containers up to date
   - Security verified: all ports bound to 127.0.0.1 only (no 0.0.0.0)

4. Ansible Configure ✓
   - Deployed web content, monitoring configs
   - Idempotency verified: re-run with --check --diff = 0 changes

5. SSH Tunnels ✓
   - Established multiplexed SSH session (PID printed)
   - Forwarding: 8080->80, 8081->8080, 3000->3000, 9090->9090

6. Validation ✓
   - App (via Traefik): HTTP 200
   - Grafana: HTTP 200 (with auth)
   - Prometheus: HTTP 200
   - Traefik Dashboard: HTTP 200

GRAFANA LOGIN IS labadmin

Log in with labadmin and your TF_VAR_grafana_admin_password. Module 1 set the username to labadmin rather than the default admin. Bob prints it in the operator card if you forget.

THE TRAEFIK DASHBOARD SHOULD NOT ASK YOU TO LOG IN

It answers HTTP 200 with no credentials. That is the accepted risk recorded in Module 1: the dashboard is reachable only through your own SSH tunnel, so it carries no auth. If your run reports 401 instead, the Step D audit put a BasicAuth middleware in front of it despite the accepted-risks block, and the password is a hash only Bob has seen. Re-check the accepted risks in Step D and remove the middleware before continuing.

The exact wording and numbers (recap counts, PIDs) will differ from run to run. What must hold on every run is fixed, however. Pre-flight passes. Every port binds only to 127.0.0.1. The --check re-run reports changed=0, and every service answers through its tunnel.

Here is the checklist as Bob Shell prints it:

Below the checklist comes the operator card, which is the part you use next. It lists every URL to open from your laptop and the Grafana login. It also carries the tear-down commands for both the tunnel and the whole stack, along with the running container count (six here: traefik, apache_web, prometheus, grafana, plus the Loki and Promtail additions from Module 1):

docs.title: vi. IF THE RUN FAILS
docs.text:
Each dropdown below is a real failure this deployment can produce, matched to the step that triggers it. Expand the one that matches your symptom.

TROUBLESHOOTING: Ansible run fails on dpkg returned an error code (1) or Rancher Desktop will not start

Cause — the server arrived broken; nothing in your code is at fault. TechZone Ubuntu images sometimes ship with a half-configured shim-signed package whose post-install script tries to mount an EFI partition that does not exist on the VM. It exits non-zero on every apt operation, so the Rancher Desktop install fails. Systemd then retries its unit until it trips its start limit and refuses to come up at all, which is a second, separate failure you must clear even after apt is healthy.

Fix — repair the host, then re-run the play. This is host state rather than repository code, so fixing it does not break the "only run it" constraint:

ssh -i "$SSH_KEY" -p $SSH_PORT ${SSH_USER}@${TARGET_HOST} '
  sudo sed -i "2i exit 0" /var/lib/dpkg/info/shim-signed.postinst
  sudo dpkg --configure -a
  sudo apt-get install -f -y
  sudo systemctl reset-failed rdd.service
  sudo systemctl start rdd.service
  systemctl is-active rdd
'

The last line must print active. The exit 0 neutralises the bootloader-signing hook, which this lab never uses — nothing else on the host depends on it.

FIRST: DIAGNOSTICS AT A GLANCE

Before chasing a specific symptom, establish the state of the platform:

# What is running on the host? (expect: traefik, apache_web, prometheus, grafana, loki, promtail)
ssh -i "$SSH_KEY" -p $SSH_PORT ${SSH_USER}@${TARGET_HOST} "docker ps --format '{{.Names}} {{.Status}} {{.Ports}}'"

# Recent logs from a container
ssh -i "$SSH_KEY" -p $SSH_PORT ${SSH_USER}@${TARGET_HOST} "docker logs traefik --tail 50"

# What is bound where on the host: every line must show 127.0.0.1, never 0.0.0.0
ssh -i "$SSH_KEY" -p $SSH_PORT ${SSH_USER}@${TARGET_HOST} "ss -tlnp | grep -E ':(80|3000|8080|9090)'"

# Are the SSH tunnels up on the laptop?
ps aux | grep 'ssh.*-L'

# Does the app answer through the tunnel?
curl -v http://localhost:8080/
STEP 1: BOB STOPS AND ASKS YOU FOR THE HOST, USER, PORT OR KEY PATH

Cause: Bob is reading ${TARGET_HOST} and friends as literal text. Pasting into a chat box never expands shell variables, no matter what you exported beforehand. Either the prompt's opening "resolve your own context" block was trimmed off the paste, or the variables really are missing from Bob's environment.

Fix: Tell Bob to look them up itself rather than answering by hand, so the values come from the same place every later command uses:

Do not ask me for those values. Read them from your own environment first:
env | grep -E '^(TARGET_HOST|SSH_USER|SSH_PORT|SSH_KEY)='
Then continue from step 1.

If that prints empty values, Bob Shell was not launched from the terminal where you exported them. Quit Bob Shell, re-export the five variables in the Bob IDE terminal, and start bob again from that same session.

Typing the values into the chat instead works for the current run, but only for the parts Bob types by hand. Any command it writes with a bare ${SSH_KEY} still resolves against the empty environment, which is why this shows up later as Permission denied (publickey).

STEP 2: permission denied while trying to connect to the Docker daemon socket

Cause: The SSH user is not in the docker group. Or it is, but the SSH session was opened before the group was added, so the session has not picked up the new membership.

Fix: The bootstrap step adds the user to the docker group; after that, the SSH session must be re-established. Disconnect and reconnect, or have Ansible run meta: reset_connection right after the group change. Then verify:

ssh -i "$SSH_KEY" -p $SSH_PORT ${SSH_USER}@${TARGET_HOST} "id | grep docker && docker ps"
STEP 3: Error: Cannot connect to the Docker daemon

Cause: Terraform's docker provider cannot reach the remote Docker daemon over SSH.

Fix: Verify direct access first:

ssh -i "$SSH_KEY" -p $SSH_PORT ${SSH_USER}@${TARGET_HOST} docker ps

If that fails, Rancher Desktop is not usable on the host yet; re-run the bootstrap step (ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini site.yml --tags bootstrap). If it works, check the provider configuration: the host must be ssh://${SSH_USER}@${TARGET_HOST}:${SSH_PORT}, with ssh_opts = ["-i", "<key>"] if your key is not in ~/.ssh/:

provider "docker" {
  host = "ssh://${var.ssh_user}@${var.target_host}:${var.ssh_port}"
  ssh_opts = [
    "-i", var.ssh_private_key_path,
    "-o", "StrictHostKeyChecking=no",
    "-o", "UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null",
    "-o", "IdentitiesOnly=yes",
  ]
}
STEP 3: terraform init: NO PROVIDER NAMED registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/docker

Cause: A child module uses docker_* resources without declaring kreuzwerker/docker in its own required_providers. Terraform falls back to the implicit hashicorp/docker, which does not exist.

Fix: Add a versions.tf to every module under modules/, with the same required_providers block as the root:

terraform {
  required_providers {
    docker = {
      source  = "kreuzwerker/docker"
      version = "~> 3.0"
    }
  }
}

Then re-run terraform init.

STEP 5: TUNNELS OPEN BUT EVERY REQUEST FAILS WITH administratively prohibited

Cause: TCP port forwarding is disabled in the host's sshd. Some TechZone images ship hardened with DisableForwarding yes or AllowTcpForwarding no. SSH login works fine, but every -L forward is rejected: curl http://localhost:8080 gets nothing and the ssh process prints channel N: open failed: administratively prohibited.

Fix: Enable forwarding on the host. Run this in a separate terminal on your laptop (not the one running Bob Shell), with the lab environment variables set:

ssh -i "$SSH_KEY" -p $SSH_PORT ${SSH_USER}@${TARGET_HOST} 'printf "DisableForwarding no\nAllowTcpForwarding yes\n" | sudo tee /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/0-lab-forwarding.conf >/dev/null && sudo sshd -t && sudo systemctl reload sshd && echo FORWARDING_ENABLED'

What it does, piece by piece:

  • Writes a drop-in file /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/0-lab-forwarding.conf containing DisableForwarding no and AllowTcpForwarding yes. The 0- prefix makes it sort first among the drop-ins, so it overrides any hardened setting that comes later.
  • sudo sshd -t test-parses the sshd configuration before anything is applied. If the config were broken it fails here, instead of reloading a bad config and locking you out of the server.
  • sudo systemctl reload sshd applies the change with a reload rather than a restart, so existing SSH sessions (including any open tunnel attempt) are not dropped.
  • echo FORWARDING_ENABLED only prints if every previous step succeeded. Seeing that word confirms the change.

Forwarding is checked when a tunnel channel opens rather than when you log in, so after this, re-run the tunnel command (or tell Bob Shell to retry step 5).

STEP 5: bind: Address already in use WHEN OPENING SSH TUNNELS

Cause: One of the local ports (8080, 8081, 3000, 9090) is already taken on the laptop.

Fix: Find the listener and kill it, or remap the local side of the forward:

lsof -i :3000

# Option A: kill the existing listener, then reopen the tunnel

# Option B: remap the local port
ssh -i "$SSH_KEY" -p $SSH_PORT -fN -L 13000:127.0.0.1:3000 ${SSH_USER}@${TARGET_HOST}
# and open http://localhost:13000 instead
STEP 6: TRAEFIK LOGS SPAM client version 1.24 is too old. Minimum supported API version is 1.40

Cause: Traefik's docker-provider client library starts at API 1.24, and modern Rancher Desktop refuses that handshake. Setting a DOCKER_API_VERSION environment variable on the container does not fix it; the library does not honour it.

Fix: Do not use Traefik's docker auto-discovery on this host. Switch to the file provider, with the routing rules rendered by Ansible into /opt/lab/traefik/dynamic/routes.yml and mounted read-only:

# Traefik static configuration
providers:
  file:
    directory: /etc/traefik/dynamic
    watch: true

As a further benefit, this removes the need to mount the Rancher Desktop socket into Traefik at all, which is better for the security review from Module 1.

STEP 6: EVERY CONTAINER IS healthy, BUT APACHE SERVES \"It works!\", TRAEFIK 404s AND GRAFANA HAS NO DASHBOARDS

Cause: /opt/lab is not mounted into the Rancher Desktop VM. Rancher Desktop runs Docker inside a Linux VM, so the daemon resolves every bind-mount source against the VM's filesystem, not the Ubuntu host's. Ansible rendered the configs on the host; the daemon looked in the VM, found nothing, and created empty directories in their place. Traefik starts with no routes, Apache falls back to its stock landing page so the grep "Welcome" check fails, Prometheus finds no scrape config, and Grafana provisions zero dashboards — while docker ps reports every container healthy. This is the most misleading failure in the lab: it looks like success.

Fix: confirm the mount from inside Rancher Desktop rather than from the host.

# On the host: the file Ansible rendered
ssh -i "$SSH_KEY" -p $SSH_PORT ${SSH_USER}@${TARGET_HOST} "cat /opt/lab/web/index.html | head -3"

# Inside Rancher Desktop: the same path, as the daemon sees it. If this is empty,
# /opt/lab is not in the VM's mount list and no bind mount in this lab works.
ssh -i "$SSH_KEY" -p $SSH_PORT ${SSH_USER}@${TARGET_HOST} \
  "docker run --rm -v /opt/lab:/check alpine ls -la /check/web"

Add /opt/lab to Rancher Desktop's VM mount list as a writable mount, restart Rancher Desktop, then re-run terraform apply and site.yml --tags content. Re-check with the second command before moving on.

STEP 7: SELF-HEAL DEMO DOES NOT FIRE, CONTAINER STAYS Exited (137)

Cause: Two separate traps:

  1. docker stop / docker kill are treated as deliberate user stops by the daemon. restart: always only fires on unexpected exits.
  2. Even docker exec apache_web kill -9 1 from inside is a no-op: Linux protects PID 1 of a PID namespace from SIGKILL. Without tini, httpd-as-PID-1 is immune.

Fix: The container must have init = true (set in Module 1, Step B) so Rancher injects tini as PID 1 and httpd runs as PID 2+. Then crash the app from inside, so the exit looks unexpected to the daemon. The full walkthrough is in Self-Healing & Recovery.

docs.title: vii. KEY TAKEAWAYS
docs.text:
• Pre-flight is terminal work: confirm the five environment variables, the project layout, the tool versions, and passwordless sudo before Bob Shell ever starts.
  • Clear the shim-signed package state on a fresh TechZone host first; the alternative is debugging two failures that look like one.
  • terraform.tfvars must exist with an absolute key path and domain = "localhost", and the Grafana password never lands in it.
  • Bob Shell must be launched from the session that exported the variables, since pasting never expands ${...} placeholders.
  • The prompt's constraints forbid editing the repository and require Bob to stop and report on failure; the run either proves each deliverable or fails.
  • Every known failure of the run has a troubleshooting entry matched to the step that produces it.

The tunnels Bob opened are still up. Continue to Testing and Troubleshooting, where you open the services in your own browser, re-prove idempotency by hand, and verify the no-public-ports security posture with ss -tlnp.

docs.title: Testing and Troubleshooting
docs.text: MODULE 2 | DEPLOY

docs.title: i. WHAT YOU WILL VERIFY
docs.text:
Christopher Bienko (AI Enablement GTM Product Manager) provides an overview of the Deploy - Testing and Troubleshooting module for the hands-on enablement. [2 min]

AI MATURITY CURVE

Take note of the division of labor in this chapter. Bob ran the validation once during deployment. Now you run it again yourself. The previous course called this the control beat: delegate the work, then verify the result before trusting it.

The single prompt from Automated Deployment continued well past apply: its step 6 validated the whole platform through the tunnels before reporting success. This page covers the part you perform yourself. You open the services in your browser, then hand Bob one follow-up prompt to re-prove the two claims that matter most: the stack is idempotent, and the host has zero public web ports.

Everything here runs against localhost on your laptop, which is precisely the design intent: the only path to the platform is the SSH tunnel Bob Shell opened in Step 5.

docs.title: ii. WHAT BOB VALIDATED
docs.text:
There is nothing to run in this section. Step 6 of the deployment prompt validated the platform. It ran four HTTP checks through the tunnels — the app, the Traefik API, Grafana, and Prometheus. It also produced a remote docker ps listing and a port audit confirming that nothing binds to 0.0.0.0. If a service misbehaves once you start browsing, the two dropdowns below cover the usual causes.

TROUBLESHOOTING: channel ... open failed: connect failed when curling localhost

Cause: The tunnel is up, but the remote container is not yet listening on 127.0.0.1. Either it is still starting, or its ports block does not bind to loopback.

Fix: Re-check what's running and listening on the host, and confirm ip = "127.0.0.1" in the Terraform ports block:

ssh -i "$SSH_KEY" -p $SSH_PORT ${SSH_USER}@${TARGET_HOST} "docker ps"
ssh -i "$SSH_KEY" -p $SSH_PORT ${SSH_USER}@${TARGET_HOST} "ss -tlnp | grep -E ':(80|3000|8080|9090)'"
TROUBLESHOOTING: localhost:8080 works but localhost:3000 does not

Cause: Grafana has not finished its first-boot database migration; the other services come up faster.

Fix: Wait 15–20 seconds and re-curl http://localhost:3000/api/health. If it persists:

ssh -i "$SSH_KEY" -p $SSH_PORT ${SSH_USER}@${TARGET_HOST} "docker logs grafana --tail 50"

docs.title: iii. VALIDATING THE PLATFORM
docs.text: After Bob Shell finishes, the tunnels are already up. Inspect the platform directly first, then hand the remaining proofs back to Bob.

docs.title: Open the services in a browser
docs.text:
open http://localhost:8080      # the app
open http://localhost:3000      # Grafana (labadmin / $TF_VAR_grafana_admin_password)
open http://localhost:8081      # Traefik dashboard
open http://localhost:9090      # Prometheus

The open command is specific for macOS. Use xdg-open on Linux.

The app's landing page, served by Apache behind Traefik. The card itself confirms the design: lab_net network, 127.0.0.1 bindings only, provisioned by Ansible + Terraform:

Grafana's login screen. Sign in with labadmin and your TF_VAR_grafana_admin_password:

The Traefik dashboard opens straight to its router and service view, with no login required. Module 1 recorded that as an accepted risk rather than a finding: the dashboard is only reachable through your tunnel, so a password on it would protect nothing while hiding the credentials from you.

TROUBLESHOOTING: the Traefik dashboard asks you to sign in

Cause: The Step D audit ignored the accepted-risks block and put a BasicAuth middleware in front of the dashboard. It generated the password hash itself, so there is no credential to type. This is the most common way the lab goes wrong.

Fix: Find the middleware and take it out, then re-apply:

grep -rn 'basicauth\|users *=' infra/terraform infra/ansible
cd infra/terraform && terraform apply

Then re-run the Step D audit with its accepted-risks block intact, so the middleware does not come back on the next pass.

Prometheus opens straight to its query page with no login required. Reachability is its protection, since the only path to it is your tunnel:

TROUBLESHOOTING: Grafana says invalid username or password

Cause: TF_VAR_grafana_admin_password was not exported in the same shell that ran terraform apply, so Grafana was provisioned with a different password than the one you are typing. (Remember also that the username is labadmin rather than admin.)

Fix: GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_PASSWORD only takes effect the first time Grafana initialises its database, and that database lives on a named volume that survives container replacement. So re-running terraform apply on its own will not change the password. Reset it in place instead:

ssh -i "$SSH_KEY" -p $SSH_PORT ${SSH_USER}@${TARGET_HOST} "docker exec grafana grafana-cli admin reset-admin-password '<your-password>'"

Then export the same value so future applies agree with it:

export TF_VAR_grafana_admin_password='<your-password>'

Log in as labadmin with that value. To start completely clean instead, remove the grafana_data volume and re-apply, which loses saved dashboards.

docs.title: Optional: have Bob re-prove the claims
docs.text:
Give Bob Shell one follow-up prompt:

Re-run terraform plan and ansible-playbook in --check mode and confirm 0 changes. Then show me that no port is bound to 0.0.0.0 on the host.

Bob runs the same commands an operator would and reports back. Read its output against what must hold:

  • terraform plan reports No changes, meaning the real infrastructure matches the code.
  • The Ansible check run finishes with changed=0 in the PLAY RECAP.
  • The port listing on the host (ss -tlnp) shows every published port on 127.0.0.1, never 0.0.0.0. The cloud security group never changed: only SSH is exposed, and the internet cannot see this platform at all.

This is what distinguishes infrastructure from a script — running it a second time does nothing, because nothing remains to converge. If Bob reports changes instead, that is drift, and the two most common causes are covered below.

Killing a container to prove self-healing belongs to Self-Healing & Recovery. This page validates; Module 3 breaks things deliberately.

TROUBLESHOOTING: terraform plan keeps showing N to add / N to destroy on a re-run

Cause: The kreuzwerker/docker provider sees the daemon-injected log_opts (from daemon.json) and the image's USER / WORKDIR defaults as drift, and they forces replacement.

Fix: Every docker_container resource needs:

lifecycle {
  ignore_changes = [log_opts, user, working_dir, command]
}

Re-apply once; after that, plan is a clean no-op.

TROUBLESHOOTING: Ansible --check reports unexpected changed

Cause: A Jinja template uses non-deterministic data (timestamps, random ids), so the rendered file differs on every run.

Fix: Pin such values to variables so the rendered output is stable, then prove it:

cd infra/ansible
ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini site.yml --check --diff --private-key "$SSH_KEY"

--diff shows exactly which lines churn; that is the template to fix.

docs.title: iv. TEARING DOWN THE TUNNEL
docs.text:
When you have finished demonstrating, terminate the multiplexed SSH session:

pkill -f "ssh.*-L 8080:127.0.0.1:80.*${TARGET_HOST}"

Matching on the forward and the host, rather than on ssh.*${TARGET_HOST} alone, means an interactive SSH session you have open to the same server survives.

If a check fails instead, there is no need to debug from scratch. It might be channel open failed on a curl, Grafana rejecting the admin password, or bind: Address already in use when the tunnel starts. Each of those has a Troubleshooting dropdown next to the step that produces it — on this page and in Automated Deployment.

docs.title: v. KEY TAKEAWAYS
docs.text:
• Bob's deployment prompt validated the platform once; the operator verifies it a second time, in person.
  • A clean terraform plan (No changes) and an Ansible check run with changed=0 are the proof of idempotency.
  • Every published port sits on 127.0.0.1, never on 0.0.0.0, and the security group exposes SSH alone.
  • The Traefik dashboard and Prometheus carry no login by design; reachability through the tunnel is their protection.
  • Grafana's admin password takes effect only at first initialization, so a mismatch is reset in place rather than re-applied.
  • Recurring plan churn and Ansible changed reports are drift, and each has a known cause documented beside the step that reveals it.

The platform is deployed and validated. Continue to Monitoring & Observability to work with the Grafana and Prometheus stack, then to Self-Healing & Recovery to crash a container and watch Rancher's restart policy bring it back.

docs.title: Monitoring and Observability
docs.text: MODULE 3 | OPERATE

docs.title: i. WHAT YOU WILL OBSERVE
docs.text:
Christopher Bienko (AI Enablement GTM Product Manager) provides an overview of the Operate - Monitoring and Observability module for the hands-on enablement. [1 min]

AI MATURITY CURVE

Take note of what this module asks of you. Bob built the observability stack in Module 1 and deployed it in Module 2. Here you verify, with your own queries, that it reports the truth. The previous course made the same demand at every stage: delegated work earns trust through evidence.

USE THE TERMINAL RATHER THAN BOB SHELL

Module 3's commands are plain shell commands. They go at the regular prompt in the Bob IDE terminal rather than into Bob Shell. If Bob Shell is still open from Module 2, exit it first. The SSH tunnels stay up: they run as a background process, independent of Bob Shell.

In this part you log into each UI and read the dashboard that was provisioned for you. You then generate traffic and watch the panels move. Finally, you query metrics and logs directly. Everything happens in two places: your browser for the UIs, and the Bob IDE terminal for the occasional command.

Everything is reached through the SSH tunnels Bob Shell opened during deployment. Nothing is publicly exposed, and there are no make targets for any of this. If the tunnels are down, reopen them as in Automated Deployment.

docs.title: ii. OPENING THE INTERFACES
docs.text:
Open each page below in its own browser tab now, and confirm each one loads before continuing. Loki is also running, but it has no page of its own. You query it through Grafana later on this page.

UI URL through the tunnel Credentials Grafana http://localhost:3000 labadmin / $TF_VAR_grafana_admin_password Prometheus http://localhost:9090 none Traefik dashboard http://localhost:8081 none The app (your traffic source) http://localhost:8080 none

YOUR LANDING PAGE MAY LOOK DIFFERENT

The landing page looks different from run to run, since Bob writes it fresh each time. That is expected; its function is the same.

Grafana

Prometheus

The app

docs.title: iii. HOW THE PIECES FIT
docs.text:
Two pipelines run side by side and never touch each other. Prometheus handles the numbers — request counts, latencies, and failure counts. Loki handles the lines: the actual log output of every container. Grafana is the only thing that sees both, and it collects nothing itself; every panel is a query it sends to one of them.

Collects Stores in You read it through Prometheus numbers scraped from /metrics endpoints Prometheus Grafana panels, or the Prometheus UI on :9090 Promtail → Loki log lines from container stdout/stderr Loki Grafana → Explore

You need both because a metric tells you that something happened and a log tells you what. When the error rate climbs, Prometheus cannot tell you which URL failed: a counter has no room for that detail. Loki has the line, GET /does-not-exist 404, with the client address and the duration.

PROMETHEUS IS THE DATABASE

Stop Prometheus and the dashboard goes blank. Stop Grafana and the data keeps accumulating regardless.

In more detail:

  • Prometheus scrapes two jobs every 15 seconds (prometheus.yml.j2): itself at localhost:9090, and Traefik at traefik:8080/metrics over the private Rancher network; no host port is involved in the scrape.
  • Grafana is provisioned from files rendered by Ansible. Two datasources are defined: Prometheus (the default, at http://prometheus:9090) and Loki (at http://loki:3100), both marked non-editable. One dashboard is loaded from /etc/grafana/dashboards.
  • Promtail discovers running containers through the Rancher socket and tails their stdout/stderr. It labels each stream with container_name, compose_service and host, then pushes to Loki. Its pipeline strips ANSI colour codes and parses the timestamp out of Traefik's access log lines so Loki stores the real log time rather than the ingest time.
  • Loki runs single-process with filesystem storage on the loki_data volume and a 31-day retention window (loki_retention_period: 744h).

There is no Alertmanager: the Prometheus template ships with the alerting: block commented out and rule_files: []. This lab visualizes; it does not page anyone.

docs.title: iv. THE PRE-PROVISIONED DASHBOARD
docs.text:
1. In the Grafana tab, log in as labadmin with your TF_VAR_grafana_admin_password.
  2. In the left sidebar, choose Dashboards → Browse.
  3. Click Traefik Overview.

This step is about understanding rather than doing. There is nothing to run here; simply read what the dashboard is already showing you.

The panels are not empty, even on a stack nobody has used yet. Prometheus scrapes Traefik every 15 seconds and Traefik pings its own healthcheck, and both of those are requests through Traefik, so Traefik counts them. Check the legend on the request-rate panel: the flat baseline series is labelled traefik, the entrypoint the monitoring stack talks to. The web entrypoint, the one a real user arrives on, sits at zero until Step 3.

A PANEL READING OF NO DATA INDICATES A BUG

Nothing here exports container or host metrics, so a panel asking for CPU or memory (container_cpu_usage_seconds_total and similar) can never have data to show. If you see one, the dashboard is querying a metric this stack does not collect. Ask Bob to fix the panel rather than assuming your platform is broken.

Bob writes this dashboard fresh on every run, so your panel titles will not match anyone else's word for word. Rather than trust a list here, read the query behind any panel yourself: hover the panel, press E, and look at the query box.

Whatever the titles say, every run shows the same four things:

  • Request and error rates come from Traefik's own counters (traefik_entrypoint_requests_total or traefik_service_requests_total, split by code). Apache exports no metrics of its own, so the Apache view is Traefik's per-service counters. Every request reaches Apache through Traefik, so nothing is missed.
  • Response time comes from histogram_quantile over ..._request_duration_seconds_bucket, usually at p50, p95 and p99.
  • Open connections come from traefik_..._open_connections.
  • Anything named for Prometheus (scrape duration, scrape samples) is Prometheus reporting on its own scraping rather than on your app.
  • A Loki logs panel, if your run built one, showing Traefik's access log lines.

docs.title: v. GENERATING TRAFFIC
docs.text:
Everything on the dashboard so far is the stack watching itself. These two loops add traffic on the web entrypoint, the path a real user takes, and deliberately break some of it.

  1. Paste this whole block into the Bob IDE terminal; the two loops run one after the other:

    # 100 successful requests
for i in {1..100}; do curl -s http://localhost:8080/ > /dev/null; done

# 20 requests to a path that doesn't exist
for i in {1..20}; do curl -s http://localhost:8080/does-not-exist > /dev/null; done

    The commands print nothing; their effect shows up on the dashboard. Each loop serves a purpose:

    • The 100 successful requests prove the whole path works end to end, laptop → SSH tunnel → host loopback → Traefik → Apache, and they separate real traffic from the monitoring noise by landing on a different entrypoint.
    • The 20 deliberate 404s give you a failure to look at. Without them the error panel stays at zero and you learn nothing from it. They also plant something specific for Loki to find in section vii, which is the difference between "errors went up" and "someone requested /does-not-exist twenty times".

  1. Switch back to the Grafana tab and set the refresh picker (top right) to 5s. Within a scrape interval or two (15 s), watch for three changes:

    • The request rate panel climbs off the floor, and the total-requests counter jumps by 120
    • The rate panel splits into two series, one for 200 and one for 404, since the second loop asked for a page that isn't there
    • The error rate panel moves off zero. If your run also has a 5xx-only panel, it stays flat: a 404 is a client error rather than a server error, and that distinction is precisely why the two are separated
    • If you have a Loki logs panel, the same requests appear in it line by line

docs.title: vi. QUERYING PROMETHEUS DIRECTLY
docs.text:
1. In the Prometheus tab (http://localhost:9090), open Status → Target health. There are two required targets, and both must show UP:

    Job Endpoint prometheus localhost:9090/metrics always traefik traefik:8080/metrics always loki loki:3100/metrics if your Step F run added a scrape job for it

    prometheus and traefik must both be UP; those two carry the whole dashboard. A third loki target is also correct — Loki reports on itself, and some runs wire up a scrape job for it in Step F. What must not appear is an exporter for Apache: Apache publishes no metrics of its own, and every request reaches it through Traefik, so Traefik's per-service counters already measure it.

    TROUBLESHOOTING: the traefik target shows DOWN

    Check the container and the metrics endpoint. Paste these into the Bob IDE terminal:

    ssh -i "$SSH_KEY" -p $SSH_PORT ${SSH_USER}@${TARGET_HOST} "docker ps | grep traefik"
ssh -i "$SSH_KEY" -p $SSH_PORT ${SSH_USER}@${TARGET_HOST} "curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/metrics | head"
  1. Run the dashboard's own queries by hand. These are the exact expressions behind the panels; running them here shows you the raw series underneath.

docs.title: Query 1: the status-code split
docs.text:
1. Paste this into the expression bar and click Execute:

    sum(rate(traefik_service_requests_total[2m])) by (code)

    The Table tab gives one row per status code, and both of your loops are visible: a 200 series from the 100 successful requests and a 404 series from the 20 requests to /does-not-exist. The result is two rows — one per outcome — split by the code label that the by (code) clause requested.

    WHY THE VALUES READ 0

    rate(...[2m]) is not a total. It is the per-second average over the last 2 minutes, so it answers "how fast are requests arriving right now" rather than "how many have there ever been". The curl loops finish in seconds, and once they are more than 2 minutes in the past the window contains no requests at all, so the rate falls to 0 for both codes.

    The rows themselves are what matter: the series still exist, which proves Traefik counted the traffic and labelled it by status code. To see non-zero values, re-run the curl loops from section v and hit Execute again within 2 minutes. For the running totals instead, drop the rate() and query sum(traefik_service_requests_total) by (code) — those numbers only ever climb.

  1. Now click the Graph tab:

    The graph is the same data over time rather than at a single instant, and it shows what the table cannot: a flat line at zero, a spike where your loops ran, then a decay back to zero. The decay is the 2-minute window sliding forward — each scrape drops a little more of the burst out of range until none of it remains. Two coloured series appear, one per status code, with the legend naming them. This shape is exactly what the request-rate panel on the Grafana dashboard draws.

docs.title: Query 2: p95 latency
docs.text:
1. Replace the expression with:

    histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(traefik_service_request_duration_seconds_bucket[2m])) by (le, service))

    This one answers a different question: how slow is the slow end of your traffic? Traefik records durations into a histogram of buckets (le = "less than or equal to"), and histogram_quantile(0.95, ...) reads across those buckets to find the response time that 95% of requests came in under. The query uses p95 rather than an average because averages hide the bad tail: a handful of slow requests barely move a mean, yet they are exactly what users notice.

    The Table view gives one row per service, with the value in seconds — so 0.0025 means 2.5 milliseconds. Expect single-digit milliseconds here: the request never leaves the host, so there is no real network latency to measure, just Traefik forwarding to Apache over the private Rancher network.

  1. Switch to Graph for the same figure over time:

    The line appears only where traffic existed and gaps where none did — histogram_quantile has nothing to compute from an empty window, so it returns no value rather than zero. A gap here means "no requests" rather than "instant responses" — a distinction worth internalizing before you read the same panel in Grafana.

docs.title: vii. QUERYING LOGS IN GRAFANA EXPLORE
docs.text: The dashboard shows a fixed Loki view; Explore is where you query the logs freely.

docs.title: Open Explore
docs.text:
1. In Grafana's left sidebar, click Explore (the compass icon).

    Explore is a scratchpad for ad-hoc queries. Unlike a dashboard panel, nothing here is saved or provisioned — you are querying the datasource directly.

  1. Choose Loki from the datasource dropdown at the top.

    It defaults to Prometheus, the default datasource for metrics. Loki holds the log lines, and the two answer different questions: Prometheus told you how many requests returned 404, Loki tells you which paths they asked for.

docs.title: Build the query with label filters
docs.text:
1. Open the label dropdown and select container_name.

    This label exists because Promtail was configured to attach it to every stream. Without it every container's logs share one undifferentiated job label and you cannot ask about a single service.

  1. Select traefik as the value.

    The dropdown lists one entry per container Promtail is tailing, which doubles as proof that log collection is working across the stack.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
1. Click Run query. The builder has assembled the LogQL you could equally have typed by hand:

    {container_name="traefik"}

  1. The results pane fills with Traefik's log lines, newest first.

    Two things are on screen. The histogram along the top bins log volume over time — the same burst you saw as a spike in Prometheus, now counted as lines rather than as a rate. Below it, the individual entries: click any line to expand its parsed fields.

    These are the same requests Prometheus counted, from the other side. The metric told you 20 requests returned 404; these lines name /does-not-exist as the path. That pairing — a number that tells you something is wrong, and a log line that tells you what — is the reason both halves exist.

  1. Run this to watch a different container entirely:

    {container_name="apache_web"}

  2. Click Live (top right), then re-run the curl loop from section v in the terminal, and watch log lines stream in as they arrive.

docs.title: viii. WHAT PERSISTS
docs.text:
CHECKLIST

Before moving on, verify the following:

  • Both Prometheus targets (prometheus, traefik) show UP
  • The curl loop moved Request Rate, the status-code split, and the error-ratio gauge
  • Access-log lines for your requests appear in the Loki panel and in Explore

All three monitoring stores sit on named Rancher volumes, so they survive container restarts and re-deploys:

  • grafana_data: Grafana's DB. Any panel you edit or add in the UI persists here (allowUiUpdates: true in the provisioning config), while the provisioned dashboard file is re-read every 30 seconds.
  • prometheus_data: the Prometheus TSDB.
  • loki_data: Loki's chunks and index, pruned by the compactor after 31 days.

Backing these volumes up and restoring them is covered in Self-Healing & Recovery.

docs.title: ix. KEY TAKEAWAYS
docs.text:
• Prometheus holds the numbers and Loki holds the lines; Grafana queries both and stores nothing of its own.
  • Traefik's per-service counters are the only application metrics, since every request reaches Apache through Traefik.
  • rate() is a per-second average over a window rather than a running total, so a burst decays back to zero as the window slides.
  • p95 latency reveals the slow tail that an average conceals, and a gap in that series means no traffic rather than instant responses.
  • The container_name label exists because Promtail was configured to attach it; without it, no single service could be isolated in Loki.
  • All three monitoring stores live on named volumes and survive container restarts and re-deploys.

Continue to Self-Healing & Recovery, where you deliberately crash the Apache container and watch Rancher's restart policy bring it back, with the dashboard you have just learned open alongside.

docs.title: Self-Healing and Recovery
docs.text: MODULE 3 | OPERATE

docs.title: i. WHAT YOU WILL DEMONSTRATE
docs.text:
Christopher Bienko (AI Enablement GTM Product Manager) provides an overview of the Operate - Self-Healing and Recovery module for the hands-on enablement. [2 min]

AI MATURITY CURVE

This closing chapter sits at the far right of the AI Maturity Curve. Bob designed the restart behavior back in Module 1, and you approved that design before it reached the server. The demonstration here is the evidence that the decision was correct. Take note that the recovery procedures remain human-run: Bob prepared the runbook, and the operator decides when to execute it.

This page covers two related topics:

  • The self-healing demo: crash the Apache container from the inside and watch restart: always bring it back, RestartCount incremented, with no human involved. This is step 7 of the Part 2 deployment prompt, and it is more subtle than it looks.
  • Recovery procedures: what to do when a restart policy is not enough. This covers rolling back a bad image, backing up and restoring the data volumes, and rebuilding from scratch.

There is no Make target for the demo. It is a short sequence of raw ssh / docker commands that you paste at the regular prompt in the Bob IDE terminal, rather than into Bob Shell — the same arrangement as Part 1. As everywhere in this lab, the service checks go through the SSH tunnels opened in Module 2 (curl http://localhost:8080), and the docker commands go over SSH to the host.

docs.title: ii. WHY A NAIVE CRASH DEMO FAILS
docs.text:
Two facts make a naive "kill the container" demo fail, and both were designed around back in Module 1.

1. docker stop and docker kill do not trigger the restart policy. Docker treats them as deliberate user stops, and restart: always fires only on unexpected exits. Stop the container from outside and it remains in the Exited (137) state indefinitely. To prove real self-healing, the crash has to come from inside the container so the exit looks unexpected to the daemon.

2. Linux protects PID 1 of a PID namespace from SIGKILL. Even from inside, docker exec apache_web kill -9 1 is a no-op: if httpd runs as PID 1, it is immune. This is why Module 1 Step B rule (e) set init = true on the web container: Rancher injects tini as PID 1 (the init flag) and httpd becomes PID 2+, which can be killed. When httpd dies, tini exits with the same status, the daemon sees an unexpected crash, and restart: always brings the container back in a few seconds.

docs.title: iii. RUNNING THE DEMO
docs.text:
THE DEMO WAS MADE POSSIBLE IN MODULE 1

Without init = true, nothing can be done at demo time to make this work — the remedy is a Terraform change and a re-apply. That single line is what makes the crash possible at all.

The demo consists of six short steps, all pasted into the Bob IDE terminal. You capture the before state and confirm the app is up. You crash it and wait. You then confirm the app is back, capture the after state, and compare.

docs.title: Capture the before state
docs.text:
1. Paste this into the Bob IDE terminal:

    ssh -i "$SSH_KEY" -p $SSH_PORT ${SSH_USER}@${TARGET_HOST} "docker inspect apache_web -f '{{.State.StartedAt}} restartCount={{.RestartCount}}'"

    It prints two things: when the Apache container last started, and how many times Rancher has restarted it since it was created.

    2026-05-04T20:46:37Z restartCount=0

    WRITE DOWN YOUR restartCount

    Your starting value depends on how many times the container has already come up; the screenshot above shows 4. The absolute number is unimportant. What matters is that it has increased by exactly 1 by the end of the demo.

    That precision is the claim being tested. Exactly +1 means Rancher saw one unexpected exit and performed one restart — a clean, controlled recovery. No change means the crash never registered as unexpected and the restart policy did not fire. More than +1 means the container is crash-looping — coming up broken and dying again each time — which is a failure that resembles a success at first glance.

    Keep this output on screen; you compare both values against it in Confirm the app is back.

docs.title: Confirm the app is up
docs.text:
1. Before breaking anything, prove it works. Otherwise a failed check afterwards tells you nothing — you would not know whether your crash caused it or whether it was already down.

    curl -fsS http://localhost:8080/

docs.title: Crash httpd inside the container
docs.text:
1. The landing page HTML prints to the terminal — look for "Welcome" in the body.

    • That output travelled the full path the lab was built around.
    • It exited your local machine and passed through the SSH tunnel into the host loopback.
    • From there it went through Traefik to Apache and returned the same way. -f makes curl fail loudly on an HTTP error instead of printing an error page, so HTML on screen means a genuine 200.

    Keep this output visible too. It is the reference you match against in Capture the after state.

    ssh -i "$SSH_KEY" -p $SSH_PORT ${SSH_USER}@${TARGET_HOST} "docker exec apache_web sh -c 'kill -9 \$(pidof httpd | tr \" \" \"\\n\" | sort -n | head -1)'"

    This reaches inside the container and kills Apache outright, without a graceful shutdown. pidof httpd lists every Apache process. The lowest PID is the parent, and kill -9 ends it immediately.

    • The command prints nothing, and that is the expected result. No confirmation message appears; the evidence that anything happened arrives in the steps that follow.
    • Inside the container, tini (PID 1) exits once its child dies, so Rancher sees the container exit unexpectedly. That is the trigger restart: always waits for.

docs.title: Wait about 10 seconds
docs.text:
1. Do nothing for the moment. Rancher notices the exit and starts the container again on its own; 8 to 12 seconds is enough.

    • This pause is the substance of the demonstration.
    • During those seconds the platform repairs itself with no human intervention whatsoever.
    • You have not run docker start, and no alert has fired.

docs.title: Confirm the app is back
docs.text:
1. Run the same curl as in Confirm the app is up:

    curl -fsS http://localhost:8080/

    • The same landing page comes back, byte for byte identical to the Confirm the app is up output, without anyone having intervened.
    • A user hitting the site during those ten seconds would have seen an error; a user arriving now sees no trace that anything went wrong.
    • If curl fails here, wait a few more seconds and try again. Apache needs a moment to bind port 80 after the container restarts.

docs.title: Capture the after state
docs.text:
1. Run the exact command from Capture the before state again:

    ssh -i "$SSH_KEY" -p $SSH_PORT ${SSH_USER}@${TARGET_HOST} "docker inspect apache_web -f '{{.State.StartedAt}} restartCount={{.RestartCount}}'"

  1. Compare it against what you noted in Capture the before state. Two things must have changed:

    Field Before After What it proves restartCount n n + 1 Rancher performed exactly one restart StartedAt original timestamp ~10 seconds later This is a new process, not the old one recovering

    A restartCount higher by exactly one is the result this demo sets out to produce. It is Rancher's own record that it detected an unexpected exit and acted upon it without a human in the loop. Self-healing is thereby demonstrated as a measured fact — and it works because of a single line written back in Module 1 Step B: init = true.

    Put together, the run looks like this (from the workshop's reference output):

    Before:  StartedAt=2026-05-04T20:46:37Z  restartCount=0
Crashed httpd inside (kill -9 inside the tini-wrapped container)
Waited 8s
After:   StartedAt=2026-05-04T20:47:29Z  restartCount=1   <- Rancher restarted it
GET http://localhost:8080/   200  <- automatic recovery confirmed
    TROUBLESHOOTING: the container stays Exited (137) and never comes back

    Two possible causes:

    • You used docker stop or docker kill from outside. The daemon treats those as deliberate user stops; restart: always is for unexpected exits only.
    • You killed PID 1 from inside (docker exec apache_web kill -9 1). Linux protects PID 1 of a PID namespace from SIGKILL; without tini, httpd-as-PID-1 is immune.

    Fix: make sure the container has init = true (set in Module 1) so Rancher injects tini as PID 1, then crash the app with the exact Crash httpd inside the container command. Restart the stopped container with docker start apache_web first if it is still down.

docs.title: iv. RECOVERY PROCEDURES
docs.text:
The restart policy handles exactly one failure mode: a crashed process. A bad image, a broken config, lost data, or a dead host each need a real recovery procedure. The essentials follow. Recall that Module 1 Step G had Bob write a full disaster-recovery runbook into your own repository at infra/RUNBOOK.md; that document describes your actual host, image tags, and volumes.

These are reference procedures for when something actually breaks rather than steps to run now. Everything below goes in the Bob IDE terminal: Terraform and Ansible commands run from the lab folder on your laptop, and anything wrapped in ssh executes on the server.

docs.title: Roll back a bad container image
docs.text:
1. The image tag is the only thing that needs to change. Edit terraform.tfvars (e.g. grafana_image = "grafana/grafana:10.4.2" back to :10.4.1), then apply with a target to limit the blast radius:

    cd infra/terraform
terraform plan -target=module.monitoring -out=rollback.plan
# The plan must show ONLY the grafana image + container being replaced.
# If any volume appears in the plan, abort and investigate.
terraform apply rollback.plan

    The operation takes about 90 seconds, and the named data volumes (prometheus_data, grafana_data, loki_data) are left untouched by a container replacement.

    If the bad change was an Ansible-rendered file instead (a broken prometheus.yml or Traefik route), restore the template from git and re-run site.yml --tags content. Traefik re-reads routes.yml automatically (file provider, watch=true); Prometheus needs a docker restart prometheus to pick up a new config.

docs.title: Back up the data volumes
docs.text:
1. Back up before any destructive operation. The pattern uses a throwaway busybox container so nothing extra needs to be installed on the host:

    ssh -p $SSH_PORT -i "$SSH_KEY" ${SSH_USER}@${TARGET_HOST} "
docker run --rm \
    -v prometheus_data:/data:ro \
    -v /var/backups/lab:/backup \
    busybox \
    tar czf /backup/prometheus_data_\$(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M%S).tar.gz -C /data .
"

  1. Repeat with grafana_data and loki_data, then scp the archives to your laptop.

    GRAFANA CANNOT BE BACKED UP LIVE

    Prometheus and Loki are mostly safe to back up while running (worst case: the last couple of minutes of data). Grafana's SQLite database is the exception: a live backup can produce a corrupt database. Always stop Grafana before backing up grafana_data.

docs.title: Restore a volume
docs.text:
1. Stop the owning container and disable its restart policy so it stays down.

    • On the server (over ssh): docker stop grafana && docker update --restart=no grafana
    • Untar the archive into the volume with the same busybox pattern as the backup, with the mounts reversed (-v grafana_data:/data -v /var/backups/lab:/backup:ro, then rm -rf /data/* && tar xzf ...)
    • Bring it back via Terraform, which also restores the correct restart policy. From infra/terraform/ on your laptop: terraform apply -target=module.monitoring.docker_container.grafana

docs.title: Full rebuild
docs.text:
1. For a new or wiped host, the whole platform comes back from code. From the project root on your laptop:

    ssh-keyscan -p $SSH_PORT $TARGET_HOST >> ~/.ssh/known_hosts
cd infra/ansible && ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini site.yml     # ~10 min cold
export TF_VAR_grafana_admin_password='...'
cd ../terraform && terraform init && terraform apply               # ~3 min
eval "$(terraform output -raw ssh_tunnel_command)"
    • Expected RTO is 15–20 minutes.
    • RPO is the age of your last volume backup — and if no backup was ever taken, the metrics, dashboards, and logs are unrecoverable.

docs.title: v. KEY TAKEAWAYS
docs.text:
• docker stop and docker kill never trigger a restart policy; the daemon treats them as deliberate stops.
  • Linux protects PID 1 from SIGKILL, so init = true — set back in Module 1 — is what makes an unexpected crash possible.
  • A restartCount higher by exactly one is the measured proof of self-healing. No change or more than one restart each signal a different failure.
  • A restart policy covers a crashed process alone. A bad image, a broken config, lost data, or a dead host each require a recovery procedure.
  • Roll back an image with a targeted plan, and abort if any volume appears in it.
  • Back up before any destructive operation, and stop Grafana first; its SQLite database cannot be backed up live.
  • A full rebuild from code carries an RTO of 15–20 minutes, and the RPO is the age of the last volume backup.

Congratulations on reaching the conclusion of the hands-on work. Step back and consider what this course has demonstrated. Bob designed a production-grade platform from a single paragraph. It generated the Terraform and Ansible, then reviewed its own work. It deployed the result to a live host and proved that the platform heals itself. At every one of those stages, you reviewed and approved before anything touched the server. That pairing is the discipline of the AI Maturity Curve applied to infrastructure, and it is precisely the story worth carrying into your next client conversation about AI-assisted DevOps.

docs.title: 1. Zero-trust networking
docs.text:
Principle: No services are exposed to the public internet.

Implementation:

  • All containers bind to 127.0.0.1 (localhost only)
  • No ports bound to 0.0.0.0 (all interfaces)
  • Access exclusively via encrypted SSH tunnels
  • Firewall only allows SSH inbound

Benefits:

  • Eliminates attack surface
  • No need for TLS certificates
  • Simplified security posture
  • Compliance-friendly

docs.title: 2. Infrastructure as code
docs.text:
Principle: All infrastructure is defined in version-controlled code.

Implementation:

  • Terraform manages Docker resources via the kreuzwerker/docker provider
  • Ansible manages host configuration
  • Git tracks all changes
  • CI/CD validates before deployment

Benefits:

  • Reproducible deployments
  • Auditable changes
  • Disaster recovery ready
  • Environment parity

docs.title: 3. Observability first
docs.text:
Principle: Comprehensive monitoring and logging from the first deployment onward.

Implementation:

  • Prometheus for metrics collection
  • Grafana for visualization
  • Loki for log aggregation
  • Pre-configured dashboards

Benefits:

  • Proactive issue detection
  • Root cause analysis
  • Performance optimization
  • SLA compliance

docs.title: 4. Self-healing
docs.text:
Principle: Automatic recovery from failures.

Implementation:

  • Docker restart policies (always)
  • Health checks on all containers
  • Init system (tini) for proper signal handling
  • Automated monitoring and alerting

Benefits:

  • Reduced downtime
  • Lower operational burden
  • Improved reliability
  • Faster recovery
