docs.title: Registration and Setup
docs.text: GETTING STARTED

docs.title: i. WHAT YOU WILL CONFIGURE
docs.text:
Christopher Bienko (AI Enablement GTM Product Manager) provides an overview of the Registration and Setup module for the hands-on enablement. [2 min]

Before beginning Module 1 | Design of the hands-on lab, three components must first be configured.

  1. A remote Ubuntu server, reserved through IBM Technology Zone (ITZ).
  2. The software and tools on your local machine: Bob IDE, Terraform and Ansible, plus a few standard utilities.
  3. A working SSH connection between Bob IDE and the ITZ remote server.

Detailed instructions on how to acquire and configure these components are provided within this hands-on section in the pages below.

docs.title: ii. RESERVING THE SERVER
docs.text:
The first order of business will be booking an Ubuntu server image via IBM Technology Zone, IBM's platform for reserving demo and lab environments. The reservation provisions an Ubuntu server for you and hands you everything needed to reach it: a public IP address and SSH port, along with a username and a private key file.

  1. Sign in at techzone.ibm.com with your IBMid, then search for the lab environment:

    IBM TECHNOLOGY ZONE COLLECTION

    URL: https://techzone.ibm.com/collection/bob-business-partner-enablement/environments

    NAME: Ubuntu VPC 24-04-04

  1. Within the Ubuntu VPC 24-04-04 tile, hover over the ibmcloud-2 environment button and click Reserve to launch the reservation configuration tool.

  1. Step 1: General of the configuration process will ask you to specify a Name and Description for your reservation. When ready, click Next in the bottom-right corner to continue.

  1. Step 2: Business purpose should be set to Learning. When ready, click Next to continue.

  1. Step 3: Deployment will ask you to specify the Geography for your deployment. Select the data center location that is closest to you. When ready, click Next to continue.

  1. Step 4: Scheduling will ask you to specify the go-live and termination dates for your entitlement. Choose a window that comfortably covers the time you expect to spend on this lab. If the entitlement lapses before you finish, you can submit a new request using these same instructions. When ready, click Next to continue.

  1. Step 5: Configure can be left unmodified. When ready, click Next to continue.

  1. Step 6: Review and submit will ask you to review your configuration settings before submitting the request. Scroll down through your reservation details and, if you approve, check the I agree to IBM Technology Zone's terms & conditions and user security policies. box at the bottom of the page. When ready, click Submit to initiate the reservation request.

  1. The web browser will redirect automatically to IBM Technology Zone's My requests dashboard. From this page, you can monitor and track the progression of your reservation request as it moves from Scheduled to Provisioning to Ready. Wait until the request is marked as Ready before advancing.

    Average deployment times are roughly 20 minutes or less.

  1. When the reservation is Ready, you will receive an email to your inbox providing you with a link to the environment and the same details will also be accessible via the My requests dashboard (where you were tracking the reservation request).

    Click either the View your request link in the email body OR click the arrow to the left of your reservation name on the My requests dashboard to expand details about the request.

  1. The environment details page contains everything the lab's environment variables need:

    Details page shows You'll use it as Public IP address TARGET_HOST SSH port (often non-standard, e.g. 2223) SSH_PORT Username (typically itzuser) SSH_USER Deployment SSH private key → ssh_private_key.pem SSH_KEY

  1. On the details page, click Download under Deployment SSH private key.

  1. Click Show ssh_private_key.pem to reveal the downloaded file.

  1. Move the .pem file into your lab folder, so that the SSH_KEY path used later in the lab can be given as ./ssh_private_key.pem.

  1. The lab folder now shows the key alongside the starter files.

    Then lock down its permissions. This .pem file is effectively the password to your server, so it should be readable by you and nobody else. SSH enforces this: if the file is readable by other accounts on your laptop, it refuses to use the key and the connection fails with an "UNPROTECTED PRIVATE KEY FILE" warning. The command below makes you the only one who can read or edit it. Run it in the Bob IDE terminal:

    chmod 600 ssh_private_key.pem

    RESERVATIONS EXPIRE

    When the reservation ends, the VSI is deleted — along with anything deployed on it. That is fine for this lab (the entire stack rebuilds from code), but extend the reservation from the details page if you need the environment longer.

docs.title: iii. SOFTWARE CONFIGURATION
docs.text: The hands-on lab you are embarking on requires that several open source tools and drivers are available on your personal (local) machine. Many of these have become ubiquitous parts of our day-to-day as technology sellers and practitioners — so it's likely you have some (if not all) of these already configured on your local machine. Ensure that you have all of these components configured before advancing to section iv. There is a verification and validation step at the end of this section (iii.) that you can leverage to sanity-check everything is working before advancing.

docs.title: Required software
docs.text:
You will require the following tools and technologies on your local machine. Instructions on acquiring and configuring each of them are detailed in the pages below.

Tool Minimum Version Purpose Installation Method Bob IDE Latest Infrastructure code generation Download from IBM Python >= 3.8 Required for Ansible System package manager Terraform >= 1.6 Infrastructure provisioning See below Ansible >= 2.15 Configuration management pip install SSH Client Any Remote server access Pre-installed (most systems) curl Any API testing Pre-installed (most systems) GNU make Any Automation scripts System package manager

docs.title: Installing Terraform
docs.text:
Follow the instruction set that matches your local machine's operating system.

macOS (Homebrew): 

brew tap hashicorp/tap
brew install hashicorp/tap/terraform

Linux (Ubuntu/Debian): 

wget -O- https://apt.releases.hashicorp.com/gpg | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /usr/share/keyrings/hashicorp-archive-keyring.gpg
echo "deb [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/hashicorp-archive-keyring.gpg] https://apt.releases.hashicorp.com $(lsb_release -cs) main" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/hashicorp.list
sudo apt update && sudo apt install terraform

Windows (Chocolatey): 

choco install terraform

Alternative (Direct Download): Download from terraform.io/downloads and add to PATH.

TROUBLESHOOTING: terraform: command not found

Cause — Terraform is not installed or not on the PATH.

Fix: 

# macOS with Homebrew
brew install terraform

# Ubuntu/Debian
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install terraform

# Verify installation
which terraform
terraform version

docs.title: Installing Ansible
docs.text:
Ansible is installed via Python's pip package manager. Use the Bob IDE terminal or your system terminal:

Install Ansible using pip: 

# Ensure pip is up to date
python3 -m pip install --upgrade pip

# Install Ansible
python3 -m pip install ansible

# Verify installation
ansible --version

Expected output: 

ansible [core 2.15.x]
  config file = None
  configured module search path = [...]
  ansible python module location = [...]
  executable location = /usr/local/bin/ansible
  python version = 3.x.x

Alternative: Install with additional tools: 

# Install Ansible with commonly used collections
python3 -m pip install ansible ansible-lint
TROUBLESHOOTING: pip: command not found

Cause — Python 3 / pip is not installed on the laptop.

Fix: 

# macOS
brew install python3

# Ubuntu/Debian
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install python3 python3-pip

# Verify
python3 --version
python3 -m pip --version
TROUBLESHOOTING: Ansible fails to install, or ansible: command not found afterwards

Cause — a system-wide pip install needs permissions you do not have, or pip's user bin directory is not on your PATH.

Fix — install into your user environment and put its bin directory on the PATH: 

python3 -m pip install --user ansible

# Add to ~/.bashrc or ~/.zshrc
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"

# Reload shell
source ~/.bashrc  # or source ~/.zshrc

docs.title: Validation and verification checks
docs.text:
Run these commands in the Bob IDE terminal to verify your setup:

# Check Python
python3 --version

# Check Terraform
terraform version

# Check Ansible
ansible --version

# Check SSH
ssh -V

# Check curl
curl --version

# Check make
make --version

EXPECTED RESULTS

  • All commands return version information — no "command not found" errors
  • Terraform >= 1.6
  • Ansible >= 2.15

docs.title: iv. WORKSPACE CONFIGURATION
docs.text:
DOWNLOAD: Lab source files

If you want to maintain a local copy of the original lab's source files on your local machine, you can do so (without a GitHub account) by downloading the following ZIP repository from Seismic.

URL: https://ibm.seismic.com/Link/Content/DChBRPJQVJQTJ8QPbp688qpPHXDd

The entire hands-on lab you are embarking on runs inside the Bob IDE, with the lab folder open as your workspace. You prompt Bob, run commands, and review generated code there. This section (iv.) ensures that the Bob IDE Workspace is properly configured before you begin.

docs.title: Launch Bob IDE
docs.text:
1. Open your computer's search.

  1. Search for IBM Bob and open it.

docs.title: Open the lab folder
docs.text:
1. On the welcome screen, click Open to browse for a workspace folder.

  1. Navigate to the DevOps-Ansible-and-Terraform folder.

  1. Click Open.

  1. Bob IDE asks whether you trust the authors of the folder. It is your own lab folder, so confirm.

    PUT THE LAB FOLDER SOMEWHERE WITH NO SPACES IN THE PATH

    A folder named IBM BOB DEV OPS (or any parent directory with a space) breaks Ansible's INI inventory, which splits host lines on whitespace. The failure is easy to miss: the inventory silently fails to parse, and Ansible falls back to implicit localhost. Every task then runs against your laptop instead of the server: templates render into your local /tmp, and the playbook appears to hang.

    Use a path like ~/labs/bob-devops instead. If you must keep a space, every inventory value holding a path has to be double-quoted, and any tool that reads it needs the same care.

docs.title: Confirm the workspace
docs.text:
1. The file explorer on the left should now show the three starter files. The folder is intentionally almost empty, since Bob generates everything else during Module 1:

    LAB/
├── README.md
├── WORKSHOP-part1-IDE.md
└── WORKSHOP-part2-CLI.md

docs.title: Open the integrated terminal
docs.text:
1. From the menu bar, click Terminal → New Terminal (or press Ctrl+` / Cmd+`).

  1. A terminal panel opens at the bottom, already inside the lab folder.

    Every command in this guide runs in this terminal, from the installs and environment variables to the SSH tests. That way it inherits the folder and the variables that Bob works with.

docs.title: Check the Bob settings
docs.text:
Open Bob's chat sidebar and set it up the way the lab expects before you prompt anything:

  1. Switch Bob to Plan mode. Module 1 starts in Plan mode. Bob proposes the design first, and you switch to Agent mode only when it is time to write files, so nothing is created until you have reviewed the plan.

    1. At the bottom right of the screen, locate the agent selection.

    2. Bob is now in Plan mode.

  1. Leave any auto-approve / autonomous-agent toggle off. Bob IDE offers a mode in which Bob applies changes or runs commands without asking. Keep it disabled for this lab.

  1. Find the "sparkle" icon (prompt enhancement). It sits on the chat box at the bottom right and needs no configuration at this stage. Module 1 uses it to expand a short prompt into a detailed one before sending.

    TROUBLESHOOTING: No "sparkle" icon within the chat box

    Prompt enhancement is turned off. Enable it:

    1. At the bottom right of the screen, click Bob settings.

    2. Click the Chat section on the settings page.

    3. Scroll to the bottom of the page and locate the Prompt enhancement section.

    4. Turn on Prompt enhancement.

    The sparkle icon now shows on the chat box.

docs.title: v. CONNECTING TO THE SERVER
docs.text:
ATTENTION: WAIT UNTIL RESERVATION IS MARKED READY

Before attempting this section (v.), wait until you receive confirmation from IBM Technology Zone that your requested environment is READY. This will arrive both as an email to your inbox and as a status update on ITZ's My requests dashboard.

With your local machine properly configured with the necessary tools and the Bob IDE Workspace prepared, it's now time to establish a connection between Bob IDE (locally) and the server reservation placed earlier from IBM Technology Zone (remotely).

docs.title: Set environment variables
docs.text:
1. Before running any commands, have these five values in front of you. The first four come from the environment details page you opened earlier (or your own server's equivalents):

    • Public IP address — of the server.
    • SSH username — Technology Zone reservations typically use itzuser.
    • SSH port — often non-standard on Technology Zone (e.g. 2223); usually 22 on other servers.
    • Path to the downloaded SSH key file — ./ssh_private_key.pem, since you moved it into the lab folder earlier.
    • A Grafana admin password — this one you invent yourself. Pick something strong; it becomes your Grafana login later in the lab.

  1. Paste each value into its command below, then run them in the Bob IDE terminal:

    export TARGET_HOST=[paste public IP here]
export SSH_USER=[paste SSH username here]
export SSH_PORT=[paste SSH port here]
export SSH_KEY=[paste path to SSH key file here]
export TF_VAR_grafana_admin_password='[type your chosen Grafana password here]'
    NOT SURE YOU FILLED THEM IN CORRECTLY? A COMPLETED SET LOOKS LIKE THIS

    These are sample values from an expired reservation — do not copy them, as they will not work. They are here only so you can compare the shape of your values:

    export TARGET_HOST=150.240.70.220
export SSH_USER=itzuser
export SSH_PORT=2223
export SSH_KEY=./ssh_private_key.pem
export TF_VAR_grafana_admin_password='Workshop!2026'

docs.title: Test SSH connectivity
docs.text:
1. Verify you can connect to the remote server with passwordless sudo:

    ssh -i "$SSH_KEY" -p $SSH_PORT ${SSH_USER}@${TARGET_HOST} 'sudo -n true && echo ok'

    Expected output: ok

    If this fails, review:

    • SSH key permissions are 600
    • SSH key is authorized on the remote server
    • User has passwordless sudo configured
    • Firewall allows SSH on the specified port
    TROUBLESHOOTING: Permission denied (publickey)

    Cause: the key file is either too permissive (SSH refuses loose keys) or not the key the server expects.

    Fix: 

    # Verify key permissions, must show -rw------- (600)
ls -la "$SSH_KEY"
chmod 600 "$SSH_KEY"

# Verify the key is a private key at all
head -1 "$SSH_KEY"
# Should start with: -----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY----- or similar
    TROUBLESHOOTING: cannot reach the remote server over SSH

    Cause — wrong host/port, the reservation is not Ready yet, or a network path problem.

    Fix — narrow it down layer by layer: 

    # Test basic connectivity
ping $TARGET_HOST

# Test the SSH port specifically
nc -zv $TARGET_HOST $SSH_PORT

# Verbose SSH connection — read the last lines before the failure
ssh -v -i "$SSH_KEY" -p $SSH_PORT ${SSH_USER}@${TARGET_HOST}
    TROUBLESHOOTING: sudo -n true asks for a password

    Cause — the SSH user does not have passwordless sudo. (The Technology Zone VSI comes with it preconfigured — this mainly affects bring-your-own servers.)

    Fix — configure it on the remote server: 

    # On the remote server:
echo "${SSH_USER} ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL" | sudo tee /etc/sudoers.d/${SSH_USER}

docs.title: vi. TROUBLESHOOTING
docs.text:

  1. Expand the Troubleshooting dropdowns under the step you are stuck on. Each known failure and its fix sits directly beneath the instruction that triggers it.
  2. Check the Reference Documentation.
  3. Verify all environment variables are set correctly.
  4. Ensure SSH connectivity before proceeding.
  5. Confirm all tools are installed and in PATH.

docs.title: vii. READY TO PROCEED
docs.text:
Setup is complete. Bob IDE is open on the lab folder with the tools installed, the server is reserved, and the SSH connection is verified. You are ready to begin the hands-on work and watch Bob design and build infrastructure as it would within a client's real project.

Before proceeding to Module 1 | Design, verify all items below:

  • Technology Zone reservation in Ready status
  • SSH key (.pem) downloaded from the reservation page
  • Bob IDE installed and authenticated
  • Lab folder opened in Bob IDE
  • Terminal accessible in Bob IDE
  • Python >= 3.8 installed
  • Terraform >= 1.6 installed
  • Ansible >= 2.15 installed (via pip)
  • SSH client available
  • Environment variables configured in terminal
  • SSH key has correct permissions (chmod 600)
  • SSH connectivity to remote server verified
  • TF_VAR_grafana_admin_password set

Proceed to Module 1 | Design, where you hand Bob a one-paragraph requirement and review the architecture it proposes.
